modules.title: Presence & Listening
modules.tagline: Be the person everyone wants to keep talking to.
modules.intro: Everything else in this course runs on presence: how you sound, when you stop talking, and how well you listen. These techniques make people open up, feel understood and lean in, at work, with friends and with your partner. Start here and use them daily.

techniques.name: Strategic Pauses and Silence
techniques.aka: The power pause, letting it land
techniques.summary: Stop talking at the moments that matter so your words land and the other person fills the space.
techniques.why: Silence after a key line gives the listener time to feel it instead of skimming past it, and it signals that you are not anxious for approval. In negotiation, most people find a gap uncomfortable and fill it with information or a better offer. Rushing to fill silence reads as nerves; holding it reads as calm confidence.
steps: Pick the one line that matters most in what you are about to say.
Say it, then stop and count three slow beats in your head.
Keep a relaxed face and soft eye contact while you wait.
After a question or an offer, let the other person speak first.
If you must break the silence, do it with a short question, not a retreat.

examples.flat: Our budget is 40k, but we could maybe stretch, I guess, if that's a problem?
examples.better: Our budget is 40k. (pause, wait)
examples.note: Stopping after the number keeps it firm and invites them to respond first.

examples.flat: So, um, I think we should probably cut the feature, if that makes sense, or not.
examples.better: I think we should cut the feature. (pause) Here's why.
examples.note: The pause marks the decision as considered, then the reason follows on your terms.

examples.flat: I missed you today, anyway, what do you want for dinner?
examples.better: I missed you today. (hold her eyes for a beat)
examples.note: Letting the line breathe turns a throwaway into a moment she actually feels.

examples.flat: You've got a great laugh, ha, sorry, that was random.
examples.better: You've got a great laugh. (smile, pause, let it sit)
examples.note: Not apologising or rushing shows you meant it and are comfortable with the compliment.

examples.flat: Any questions? No? Okay, great, moving on.
examples.better: Any questions? (count five, look around the room)
examples.note: Real questions usually come after the awkward three seconds most presenters skip.

examples.flat: That's rough, but at least you can find another job, right?
examples.better: That's rough. (pause) What happened?
examples.note: The pause shows you are taking it in before jumping to fix it.

examples.flat: Is that your best price? Because if not, that's fine, we can talk.
examples.better: Is that your best price? (silence)
examples.note: Waiting quietly after the question often produces a better number than any argument.

examples.flat: Close your eyes. Okay, open them, surprise!
examples.better: Close your eyes. (long pause) Keep them closed. (pause) Now.
examples.note: Stretching the gap builds anticipation, which is half the fun of a surprise.

mistakes: Filling the gap with qualifiers like 'if that's okay' that undo the point.
Pausing with a tense face or fidgeting, which reads as freezing rather than calm.
Using silence as a punishment or stonewalling in a conflict.
Pausing so often that every sentence feels like a performance.

drills.prompt: Rewrite with a pause in the right place: 'I'd like a raise, I mean, if the budget allows, I know things are tight.'
models: I'd like to talk about a raise. (pause) I've taken on the Lyon account and the team lead role.
Based on the last year, I'm asking for a raise to 62k. (pause and wait)

drills.prompt: Your partner asks 'Do you still find me attractive?' Write a reply that uses a pause well.
models: (look at her for a beat) Yes. (pause) Very.
(slow smile) Come here and I'll answer properly.

quiz.scenario: You've just stated your asking price to a buyer. They frown and say nothing. What do you do?
options: Lower the price slightly to ease the tension
Explain all the features again
Ask if they're unhappy with it
Stay quiet and relaxed and let them respond
quiz.why: The first person to fill the silence usually gives ground. Calm silence keeps your number intact.

quiz.scenario: Which moment is the best place for a deliberate pause in a toast?
options: Right after the line you most want people to remember
Before you say your name
In the middle of a joke's setup
Between every sentence
quiz.why: One well-placed pause after the key line makes it land; pausing everywhere dilutes it.

techniques.ethics: Silence that gives people room to think or feel is respectful; silence used to punish or freeze someone out is the stonewalling Gottman warns against.

techniques.name: Tone and Pace
techniques.aka: Late-night FM DJ voice, downward inflection, the calm voice
sources: Klofstad, Anderson & Peters, Sounds like a winner (2012)
techniques.summary: Speak slower, lower and with a downward finish when you want to sound calm and sure, and lighter and warmer when you want to invite.
techniques.why: Listeners judge confidence and trustworthiness from how you sound before they weigh what you say. Research links lower-pitched voices with perceived strength and competence, and a slow, steady pace signals you are not under pressure. Rising at the end of a statement turns it into a request for permission; a downward finish closes it.
steps: Before an important line, breathe out and drop your shoulders.
Slow down to about two thirds of your normal speed.
End statements on a falling note, not a rising one.
Use a warmer, slightly playful tone for invitations and a flat calm one for limits.
Record yourself once and listen for uptalk and rushing.

examples.flat: We can't go below 50? (rising, fast)
examples.better: We can't go below fifty. (slow, falling)
examples.note: The same words with a downward finish sound like a fact, not a hope.

examples.flat: So I was thinking maybe we could, like, try the new process?
examples.better: Let's try the new process for two weeks. (calm, even)
examples.note: A steady pace and falling tone turn a suggestion into a plan people follow.

examples.flat: Hey, wanna go to bed early tonight?
examples.better: (low, slow, close to her ear) Early night tonight.
examples.note: Slowing down and lowering your voice changes the meaning without changing much of the wording.

examples.flat: So, um, do you wanna maybe get a drink sometime?
examples.better: I'd like to take you for a drink on Thursday. (relaxed, warm)
examples.note: An unhurried tone says you'd enjoy it, not that you're bracing for rejection.

examples.flat: WHY is there mud all over the floor?!
examples.better: (quiet, slow) Okay. Shoes off at the door, please. Then we'll clean this together.
examples.note: A calm low voice de-escalates where a raised one invites a fight.

examples.flat: Sorry, sorry, this'll be quick, I just need two minutes?
examples.better: I need two minutes on the launch date. (pause) Now's good?
examples.note: Measured pace signals your request is worth the time, so people give it.

examples.flat: No, I can't come, sorry, I'm so sorry, it's just a lot this week.
examples.better: I can't make it this week. (warm) Next one, I'm in.
examples.note: A warm, settled 'no' sounds kind and final, without the anxious over-apology.

examples.flat: I've got a surprise for you later!! (fast, excited)
examples.better: (slow, half-smile) I've got something planned for later. You'll see.
examples.note: A slower, quieter delivery builds curiosity instead of spending it all at once.

mistakes: Going so low and slow that it sounds like an impression or a movie trailer.
Using the calm voice to sound superior or dismissive in an argument.
Uptalking through every sentence, which makes even good points sound unsure.
Matching an angry person's volume instead of staying steady.

drills.prompt: Say this two ways and write stage directions for the better one: 'I think I deserve the lead role on this project.'
models: (slow, falling finish) I'm the right person to lead this project. (pause)
(even, warm) I want to lead this project, and here's the plan I'd run.

drills.prompt: Rewrite for a calm, low delivery: 'OMG we have to go to that new place, it's going to be SO good, please please please?'
models: (relaxed) There's a new place I want to take you. Friday.
(slow, playful) I found somewhere you're going to like. I'll pick you up at eight.

quiz.scenario: A colleague is angry and talking fast and loud at you. Which response best calms things?
options: Match their energy so they know you care
Talk faster to get your side in
Answer slowly and quietly with a falling tone
Stay silent and walk away
quiz.why: A slow, low voice is contagious; people tend to come down to your level.

quiz.scenario: Which delivery of 'The deadline is Friday' sounds most certain?
options: Fast, with a rising finish
Slow, with a falling finish
Loud, with emphasis on every word
Soft, followed by 'is that okay?'
quiz.why: A falling finish marks a statement as settled; rising endings and tag questions invite pushback.

techniques.ethics: Using a calm voice to lower the temperature and be understood is fair; using it to sound condescending or to talk over someone's real distress is not.

techniques.name: Mirroring
sources: Maddux, Mullen & Galinsky, Chameleons bake bigger pies (2008)
van Baaren et al., Mimicry and prosocial behavior (2004)
techniques.summary: Repeat the last one to three key words someone said, with a curious tone, so they keep talking.
techniques.why: Hearing their own words back tells people you are listening and invites them to expand without you steering. Studies find that subtle verbal and behavioural mimicry increases liking and helps negotiators reach better deals. It also buys you time to think while they give you more information.
steps: Listen for the last few words that carry the meaning.
Repeat them back with a slight upward, curious tone.
Then go silent and let them expand.
Use it two or three times in a conversation, not every turn.
Mix with labels and questions so it doesn't sound robotic.

examples.flat: Okay, why is the timeline a problem?
examples.better: The timeline doesn't work for legal? ...
examples.note: Echoing their phrase gets them to explain the real constraint without feeling interrogated.

examples.flat: That's ridiculous, that price is fine.
examples.better: Too high for this quarter?
examples.note: Mirroring their objection uncovers whether the issue is price or timing.

examples.flat: Oh cool. So, what else do you do?
examples.better: You secretly want to open a bakery?
examples.note: Picking up the most interesting words shows you were actually listening and invites the story.

examples.flat: Okay. Do you want to talk about it?
examples.better: He said that in front of everyone?
examples.note: A mirror lets her vent at her own pace instead of being pushed to 'talk about it'.

examples.flat: Ugh, that sucks. Anyway...
examples.better: Your landlord just turned up?
examples.note: Repeating the striking detail keeps the story going and shows you're with them.

examples.flat: lol nice
examples.better: you climbed it in the rain??
examples.note: In text, a mirror with surprise reads as engaged, unlike a generic reaction.

examples.flat: What do you mean by that?
examples.better: It feels rushed?
examples.note: Shorter and warmer than a demand for clarification, and it gets the same detail.

examples.flat: Okay, I'll stop then.
examples.better: You like it when I'm slow?
examples.note: A playful mirror turns a passing comment into flirtation and checks in at the same time.

mistakes: Parroting long sentences word for word, which feels like mockery.
Mirroring with a flat or sarcastic tone.
Mirroring every line until it feels like a technique.
Rushing to talk again instead of letting the silence after the mirror do the work.

drills.prompt: Your boss says: 'I'm worried this project will slip again.' Write a mirror.
models: Slip again?
Worried it'll slip?

drills.prompt: On a date she says: 'I almost moved to Lisbon last year, but I chickened out.' Write two different mirrors.
models: You chickened out?
Almost moved to Lisbon?
Lisbon?

quiz.scenario: A client says, 'We had a bad experience with the last agency.' Which reply is a mirror?
options: Sorry to hear that.
A bad experience?
We're not like them.
What agency was it?
quiz.why: Repeating 'a bad experience' with curiosity invites them to explain without you defending yourself.

quiz.scenario: What should you do right after delivering a mirror?
options: Add your own opinion
Ask a second question
Stay quiet and let them continue
Change the subject
quiz.why: The silence after a mirror is where they fill in the detail.

techniques.ethics: Mirroring to understand someone is fair; using it to look interested while you only wait to extract something is hollow, and people notice.

techniques.name: Labeling Emotions
sources: Lieberman et al., Putting feelings into words (2007)
techniques.summary: Name the feeling you notice in the other person, out loud and tentatively: 'It sounds like...', 'It seems like...'.
techniques.why: Putting a feeling into words tends to reduce its intensity, which lab work on affect labeling has shown. A label also proves you've understood, which lowers defences and makes people more willing to cooperate. Saying 'it sounds like' rather than 'I hear that you' keeps the focus on them and makes it easy to correct if you're wrong.
steps: Notice the emotion under the words: frustration, worry, excitement, pride.
Start with 'It sounds like', 'It seems like' or 'It looks like'.
Name the feeling, not a judgement about them.
Pause and let them confirm or correct.
For negatives, label early; for positives, label to amplify.

examples.flat: Calm down, it's not a big deal.
examples.better: It sounds like this landed on you with no warning.
examples.note: Naming the cause of the frustration calms it far better than telling someone to calm down.

examples.flat: I understand where you're coming from, but...
examples.better: It seems like you've been burned on contracts like this before.
examples.note: A specific label shows real understanding and surfaces the true objection.

examples.flat: Why are you being so quiet?
examples.better: You seem a bit far away tonight.
examples.note: A gentle label invites her to share rather than defend herself.

examples.flat: Cool job.
examples.better: You light up when you talk about the restoration work.
examples.note: Labeling a positive emotion makes people feel seen and want to say more.

examples.flat: Stop whining, we're going.
examples.better: It sounds like you really wanted to stay at the park.
examples.note: Kids, like adults, settle faster once the feeling is named.

examples.flat: At least you get a fresh start!
examples.better: That sounds exhausting, honestly.
examples.note: Skipping the silver lining and naming the feeling is what actually comforts.

examples.flat: you ok?
examples.better: sounds like today really got to you
examples.note: A label in text reads as attentive rather than a box-ticking check-in.

examples.flat: You're cute when you're impatient.
examples.better: Seems like someone's been thinking about tonight all day.
examples.note: A playful label names the anticipation and turns it up.

mistakes: Saying 'I hear you' or 'I understand', which is about you, not them.
Labeling a judgement ('You're being irrational') instead of a feeling.
Labeling with a 'but' right after, which cancels it.
Insisting your label is right when they correct you.

drills.prompt: Your colleague says: 'Third time this month the specs changed. Whatever, I'll redo it.' Write a label.
models: It sounds like you're tired of doing the same work twice.
Seems like the goalposts keep moving on you.

drills.prompt: Your partner comes home, drops her bag and sighs. Write a label, then a follow-up.
models: Looks like it was a long one. (pause) Want to tell me or want a glass of wine first?
You seem wiped out. Sit, I'll make tea.

quiz.scenario: A customer says, 'I've been on hold for forty minutes!' Which reply is the best label?
options: I understand your frustration, but our lines are busy.
Please calm down.
That's not my fault.
It sounds like you've been kept waiting far too long.
quiz.why: It names their experience without a 'but' and without making it about you.

quiz.scenario: Which opener is a label rather than a judgement?
options: It seems like you're worried about the cost.
You're overreacting about the cost.
You always complain about cost.
Why are you worried about the cost?
quiz.why: It tentatively names a feeling and leaves room to be corrected.

techniques.ethics: Naming feelings to understand and calm is emotional intelligence; naming them to diagnose, belittle or steer someone ('you're just insecure') crosses into manipulation.

techniques.name: Calibrated How and What Questions
sources: Huang et al., It doesn't hurt to ask (2017)
techniques.summary: Ask open questions starting with 'how' or 'what' that make the other person solve the problem with you.
techniques.why: A 'how' or 'what' question hands the other person the job of thinking through your constraint, so their solution feels like their idea. It avoids the accusing edge that 'why' often carries. Research also shows that people who ask more questions, especially follow-ups, are liked more.
steps: Swap 'Can you...' and 'Why did you...' for 'How' and 'What'.
Aim the question at the problem, not the person.
Use 'How am I supposed to do that?' gently to say no without saying no.
Follow up on their answer with a second open question.
Keep your tone curious, never sarcastic.

examples.flat: That price is way too high, lower it.
examples.better: How am I supposed to make that work on our budget?
examples.note: It says no while asking them to help solve the gap.

examples.flat: Why did you miss the deadline?
examples.better: What got in the way on this one?
examples.note: Removes the blame from the question so you get the real reason.

examples.flat: Can you finish this by Monday?
examples.better: What would it take to have this by Monday?
examples.note: Invites them to name the trade-off instead of a reluctant yes.

examples.flat: Do you like your job?
examples.better: What's the best part of your week usually?
examples.note: Open questions give someone room to show you who they are.

examples.flat: Did you have a good day?
examples.better: What was the best bit of today?
examples.note: A specific open question gets a story instead of 'fine'.

examples.flat: Do you want to do something this weekend?
examples.better: What would make this weekend feel like a proper escape for you?
examples.note: Puts her in the role of dreaming it up, which is half the anticipation.

examples.flat: Why can't you keep your room clean?
examples.better: What would make it easier to keep your room tidy?
examples.note: Turns a nag into a problem you solve together.

examples.flat: Are you going to break up with him?
examples.better: What do you want to happen next?
examples.note: Lets them reach their own conclusion, which they'll actually act on.

mistakes: Using 'why', which often sounds like an accusation.
Asking yes/no questions that end the conversation.
Asking 'How could you do this?', which is a 'how' question that is really an attack.
Firing questions without listening to the answers.

drills.prompt: Rewrite as a calibrated question: 'Why haven't you sent the report yet?'
models: What's holding up the report?
How are we looking on the report?

drills.prompt: A landlord says the rent is going up 15%. Write two calibrated questions.
models: How did you arrive at fifteen percent?
What would make it worth it for you to keep a reliable tenant at the current rate?

quiz.scenario: You want a supplier to cut a delivery fee. Which line works best?
options: Why are your fees so high?
Can you drop the fee?
What flexibility do you have on the delivery fee?
Your competitor charges less.
quiz.why: A 'what' question invites them to look for room rather than defend the price.

quiz.scenario: Which question is calibrated, not an attack in disguise?
options: How could you forget again?
What would help you remember next time?
Why do you always forget?
Did you forget again?
quiz.why: It focuses on a solution and carries no blame.

techniques.ethics: Calibrated questions that help both sides find a solution are fair; questions used as leading traps to corner someone are not.

techniques.name: Using Names and Their Words
sources: Carnegie, How to Win Friends and Influence People (1936)
techniques.summary: Use the other person's name once at a key moment and reuse their own words and phrases instead of translating them into yours.
techniques.why: Our own name grabs attention more reliably than almost any other word, and well-timed use signals that you see them as a person. Reusing someone's exact vocabulary shows you listened and makes your point feel familiar and agreeable to them. Their words also carry their values, so you speak in terms they already care about.
steps: Learn and say the name early; repeat it once in your head.
Use it once at a moment that matters: a greeting, a thank you, a key ask.
Note the distinctive words they use for their goals and problems.
Echo those words back when you summarise or propose.
For a partner, use a private nickname sparingly so it stays special.

examples.flat: Thanks for that, everyone.
examples.better: Priya, that point about churn changed my mind.
examples.note: Naming the person and their specific contribution makes the thanks real.

examples.flat: Our solution improves operational efficiency.
examples.better: You said your team is drowning in manual reports. This gets them out of that.
examples.note: Using their phrase 'drowning in manual reports' makes the pitch about their pain.

examples.flat: Nice to meet you.
examples.better: Nice to meet you, Elena. (later) Elena, you have to tell me the rest of that story.
examples.note: Remembering and using her name early sets you apart from people who forget it.

examples.flat: Love you, bye.
examples.better: (on the way out, quietly) Hey, Sam. You're gorgeous.
examples.note: Saying her name before the compliment makes it feel aimed and personal.

examples.flat: So you want a change of scene?
examples.better: So you want to 'get out of the hamster wheel'. What would that look like?
examples.note: Repeating his exact phrase shows you heard it the way he meant it.

examples.flat: Mom, I'll handle it.
examples.better: Mom, you said you want this Christmas to be 'calm for once'. I'll do the cooking.
examples.note: Using her own words links your offer to what she already wants.

examples.flat: sounds good
examples.better: sounds good, Dan. see you at 7
examples.note: A name in a short text adds warmth with almost no effort.

examples.flat: Did you have fun?
examples.better: You said the band would be 'pure chaos'. Was it?
examples.note: Callbacks to her words show you remember what she says, which is quietly attractive.

mistakes: Using the name in every sentence, which sounds like a sales script.
Getting the name wrong and not checking.
Translating their words into jargon so they no longer recognise their own idea.
Using a pet name in public that your partner finds embarrassing.

drills.prompt: A client says: 'We just want to stop firefighting every Monday.' Write your proposal opener using their words.
models: If the goal is to stop firefighting every Monday, here's what I'd change first.
Let's start with the thing that causes the Monday firefighting.

drills.prompt: You've just met someone at a party called Marco who said he 'lives for long weekends in the mountains'. Write a reply 10 minutes later that uses both his name and his words.
models: Marco, you said you live for long weekends in the mountains. Where's the one place I should go?
Okay Marco, mountain guy, settle this for us.

quiz.scenario: When is the best moment to use someone's name in a meeting?
options: In every sentence
When giving specific credit or making a key request
Only when you've forgotten their point
Never, it's too informal
quiz.why: One well-placed use at a moment that matters adds warmth without sounding scripted.

quiz.scenario: Your partner says she wants 'a slow Sunday with zero plans'. What's the best reply?
options: Let's do a productive Sunday instead.
We could go hiking and brunch and see friends.
Okay.
A slow Sunday with zero plans. Done. I'll bring coffee to you.
quiz.why: Repeating her exact words shows you heard her and makes the plan feel like hers.

techniques.ethics: Using names and words to show you listened is respectful; using them as a scripted trick to fake intimacy cheapens both.

techniques.name: Open Loops and Curiosity Hooks
techniques.summary: Open a question in someone's mind and hold back the answer a little, so they want to keep listening or come back for more.
techniques.why: Curiosity is triggered by a gap between what we know and what we want to know, and that gap feels like a mild itch that wants scratching. A hook that opens a small gap holds attention far better than giving everything up front. In a relationship, a little mystery and anticipation keep desire alive.
steps: Decide what the payoff is before you tease it.
Open the loop with a specific, intriguing detail, not a vague 'guess what'.
Delay the answer a short time: a minute, a slide, an evening.
Always close the loop and make the payoff worth it.
In romance, tease plans, not insecurities.

examples.flat: Today I'll cover our Q3 results.
examples.better: One number in Q3 surprised all of us. I'll show you in five minutes.
examples.note: A specific promise keeps the room listening through the setup.

examples.flat: I booked dinner at Rosa's for Saturday.
examples.better: Keep Saturday night free. Wear the green dress. That's all you get.
examples.note: A small, specific tease fills the week with anticipation.

examples.flat: had a funny day lol
examples.better: remind me to tell you what happened with the pigeon at lunch
examples.note: A concrete teaser gives her a reason to ask and keeps the thread alive.

examples.flat: I work in insurance, it's boring.
examples.better: I spend my days figuring out what happens when things go badly wrong. Ask me about the boat.
examples.note: Turning a dull answer into a hook invites the next question.

examples.flat: Want to fool around later?
examples.better: (text at 2pm) I've been thinking about you since this morning. I'll tell you why tonight.
examples.note: Suggestive, not explicit, and the delay builds the tension through the afternoon.

examples.flat: Here's an email about the new process.
examples.better: Subject: The one change that saves you a Friday every month
examples.note: A benefit-led curiosity gap gets the email opened and read.

examples.flat: We went to Spain, it was fun.
examples.better: Spain was great, apart from the night we accidentally crashed a wedding.
examples.note: A dangled detail makes your story the one people ask for.

examples.flat: Here's our proposal.
examples.better: Before the numbers, there's one option your team probably hasn't considered.
examples.note: A hook keeps them engaged to hear the alternative instead of skipping to price.

mistakes: Never closing the loop, which feels like a bait and switch.
Over-hyping a payoff that turns out to be dull.
Using 'guess what' or 'you'll never believe' without a specific detail.
Teasing by withholding affection or making a partner anxious.

drills.prompt: Turn this into a hook: 'I want to talk about our marketing spend.'
models: We spent 40% of our budget on a channel that brought in 3% of customers. Let's fix that.
There's one line in our marketing spend I can't explain. Can you?

drills.prompt: Write a midday text to your partner that opens a playful loop about tonight, PG-13.
models: Don't make plans after dinner. I have an idea and you're going to like it.
I'll be home at seven. Lose the phone at eight. More details in person.

quiz.scenario: Which presentation opener creates the strongest curiosity gap?
options: Today I'll talk about churn.
Churn is important for all of us.
Let me show you some data.
We lost our biggest client last year for a reason nobody in this room has guessed.
quiz.why: It opens a specific, relevant gap that only the talk can close.

quiz.scenario: You teased your partner about a surprise all week. What matters most now?
options: That the payoff is real and thoughtful
That you keep teasing for another week
That you deny there was a surprise
That you tell everyone else first
quiz.why: An open loop only builds trust and excitement if you close it with something worth the wait.

techniques.ethics: Curiosity hooks that deliver are fair; clickbait that never pays off, or keeping someone anxious and guessing about your feelings, is manipulation.

modules.title: Persuasion
modules.tagline: Get to yes in ways people are glad you used.
modules.intro: The core, well-researched principles that move people: giving first, consistency, social proof, credibility, honest scarcity, framing, reasons, autonomy and story. Use them to make good ideas easy to say yes to, in negotiations, at work and at home. Each one has a dark twin, so read the ethics lines.

techniques.name: Reciprocity: Give First
sources: Regan, Effects of a favor and liking on compliance (1971)
Strohmetz et al., Sweetening the till (2002)
techniques.summary: Give something genuinely useful first, with no strings, and people naturally want to return the favour.
techniques.why: The urge to repay what we receive is one of the most reliable social norms across cultures. Experiments show small unsolicited gifts, like a soft drink or a mint, raise compliance and tips, especially when the gift feels personal and unexpected. Giving first also signals generosity and good faith, which builds trust.
steps: Find something the other person actually values: time, information, help, a small kindness.
Give it first, without attaching a request.
Make it personal and, if you can, unexpected.
Let some time pass before asking for anything.
When you do ask, keep it in proportion to what you gave.

examples.flat: Hey, can you review my deck?
examples.better: I noticed your report had a broken chart link, so I fixed it. (later) Would you look over my deck when you get a sec?
examples.note: A genuine favour first makes the later ask feel like an exchange between colleagues.

examples.flat: We want a 10% discount.
examples.better: We can sign a two-year term, which gives you stable revenue. In return, can you do 10%?
examples.note: Leading with a concession on their priority invites one on yours.

examples.flat: Can you watch my match with me tonight?
examples.better: (Saturday) Booked your favourite spa slot, my treat. (Sunday) Fancy watching the match with me?
examples.note: Giving something she loves first makes your request feel easy to say yes to.

examples.flat: So, what do you do?
examples.better: I'll go first: I once got lost in IKEA for two hours. Your turn, most embarrassing moment.
examples.note: Opening up first invites her to open up too; disclosure is reciprocal.

examples.flat: Can you help me move Saturday?
examples.better: I've got pizza and beer for anyone who helps me move Saturday, and I owe you one for real.
examples.note: Offering something up front makes the favour feel fair.

examples.flat: You never call.
examples.better: (sends a photo of the kids with a note) Thought you'd like this. Call when you're free?
examples.note: Giving something warm first gets a call far more often than a guilt trip.

examples.flat: Buy our software.
examples.better: Here's a free checklist we use to audit onboarding. Happy to walk you through it.
examples.note: Useful free help builds goodwill and shows competence before any pitch.

examples.flat: can u send me those photos
examples.better: sending you the good ones from saturday first, can you send me yours?
examples.note: Giving first in a small way makes the swap natural.

mistakes: Giving with obvious strings attached, which feels like a transaction or a bribe.
Keeping score out loud ('After everything I did for you...').
Asking for something far bigger than what you gave.
Giving generic gifts that cost you nothing in thought.

drills.prompt: You want a busy senior colleague to mentor you. Write a first message that gives before it asks.
models: Saw you're presenting on pricing next week. I pulled together competitor price sheets, attached in case it helps.
Loved your talk on retention. I tried your churn framework on our data, results attached.

drills.prompt: You want your partner to come to your work dinner she finds boring. Write a give-first approach.
models: I'll do the whole week of school runs. And I'd love you there Thursday, it's better with you.
Your pick of restaurant for Saturday, no complaints from me. Can I steal you for my work thing on Thursday?

quiz.scenario: Which gift is most likely to trigger reciprocity?
options: A generic company pen handed to everyone
A discount in exchange for signing today
A personal favour they didn't expect
A promise to help later
quiz.why: Personal, unexpected and already delivered: the three features that make reciprocity strongest.

quiz.scenario: Your friend helped you last month and now asks a small favour. They say, 'No pressure.' What's the healthiest frame?
options: Help because you want to and it's fair
Refuse, they're manipulating you
Help, then remind them they owe you
Ask for something bigger in return
quiz.why: Reciprocity is healthy when it's freely given and not weaponised or scored.

techniques.ethics: Giving freely and letting goodwill grow is fair; giving to create a debt and then cashing it in, or guilt-tripping with past favours, is manipulation.

techniques.name: Commitment and Consistency
techniques.aka: Small yeses, foot in the door
techniques.summary: Start with small agreements that point the way you want, because people like to act in line with what they've already said and done.
techniques.why: Once we state a position or take a step, we tend to act consistently with it to keep a stable self-image. The classic foot-in-the-door studies found people who agreed to a tiny request were far more likely to agree to a larger related one. Commitments that are active, public and freely chosen stick best.
steps: Find a small, honest step in the direction you want.
Get agreement on shared goals or values first.
Ask them to say or write the commitment in their own words.
Build to the bigger request gradually and keep it related.
Make sure every yes is genuinely free.

examples.flat: Will you lead the whole migration?
examples.better: Would you sketch what a migration plan could look like? (next week) You've got the plan, want to run it?
examples.note: A small first step makes the larger role feel like the natural next move.

examples.flat: Sign the contract today.
examples.better: We agree the goal is cutting your support costs by a third, right? (yes) Then let's look at how.
examples.note: Agreement on the goal makes the proposal a consistent next step.

examples.flat: We should exercise more.
examples.better: What if we just walk after dinner tonight? Ten minutes.
examples.note: A tiny shared yes starts the habit far better than a big plan.

examples.flat: Want to go out with me?
examples.better: You said you've never had proper ramen. That's a problem I can fix. Thursday?
examples.note: Builds on something she already said she wanted.

examples.flat: You have to do your homework now.
examples.better: What time do you want to start homework, five or half five? (later) You said five, it's five.
examples.note: Kids keep commitments they made themselves more than ones imposed.

examples.flat: You should really start that business.
examples.better: What's one tiny thing you could do this week toward it? Say it out loud.
examples.note: A stated small step is far more likely to happen.

examples.flat: Everyone please be on time.
examples.better: Can we agree as a team that we start at :00 sharp? Show of hands.
examples.note: A public, shared commitment changes behaviour more than a reminder.

examples.flat: You never plan date night.
examples.better: Let's each take one Friday a month to plan. You pick first or second?
examples.note: A concrete, chosen commitment replaces a complaint with a plan.

mistakes: Getting a yes under pressure, which won't stick and breeds resentment.
Jumping from a tiny request to an unrelated huge one.
Using their past words as a trap ('You said you'd do anything').
Asking leading yes questions that feel like a sales script.

drills.prompt: You want your team to adopt code reviews. Write a small first step that gets a yes.
models: Can we try reviews on just the payment module for two weeks and see?
Would each of you be willing to review one PR this week?

drills.prompt: Write a small first ask to get your partner on board with a weekend away she's unsure about.
models: Can we just look at a couple of places together tonight, no booking?
Pick the one place you'd say yes to if we went.

quiz.scenario: Which first step best uses commitment and consistency to get a friend to start running?
options: Sign up for a marathon today
Agree to a single short jog together on Saturday
Watch a documentary about runners
Promise to never skip a run
quiz.why: A small, specific, freely chosen action builds the self-image of 'someone who runs'.

quiz.scenario: A salesperson gets you to say yes three times to obvious questions, then pushes for a signature. What's going on?
options: Honest rapport building
A calibrated question
Reciprocity
Commitment pressure used as a script
quiz.why: Stacking hollow yeses to corner someone is the manipulative twin of genuine commitment.

techniques.ethics: Helping people act on goals they truly hold is fair; trapping them with hollow yeses or turning past words into a cage is manipulation.

techniques.name: Social Proof
sources: Goldstein, Cialdini & Griskevicius, A room with a viewpoint (2008)
techniques.summary: Show that people like them are already doing it, especially when they're uncertain.
techniques.why: When unsure what to do, we look at what similar others do. In a well-known hotel study, telling guests that most previous guests in their room reused towels beat a standard environmental appeal. The closer the comparison group is to the listener, the stronger the pull.
steps: Find real numbers or stories of people similar to the listener.
Say what most people do, not how many people fail.
Make the group as close as you can: same team, same city, same situation.
Pair it with a specific example or a name.
Never invent figures or testimonials.

examples.flat: Please fill in the survey.
examples.better: Most of the team filled the survey in by Wednesday. Takes about four minutes.
examples.note: A descriptive norm about their own team nudges the stragglers.

examples.flat: Our product is really good.
examples.better: Three other clinics your size in this region switched last year. Happy to put you in touch with one.
examples.note: Similar, checkable peers are far more persuasive than self-praise.

examples.flat: Let's try that salsa class.
examples.better: Tom and Ana did that salsa class and haven't stopped talking about it. Want to try one?
examples.note: Friends you both like make the idea feel safe and fun.

examples.flat: You should come to the run club.
examples.better: Half the people there were total beginners when they started. Nobody's fast.
examples.note: Shows people like him already joined, reducing the fear of not fitting in.

examples.flat: Everyone else is tidier than you.
examples.better: Most of your cousins do their own laundry by 14. Want me to show you?
examples.note: A positive norm framed as an invitation, not a put-down.

examples.flat: So many people miss the expense deadline!
examples.better: 92% of people submitted expenses on time last month.
examples.note: Highlighting the majority who comply avoids normalising the failure.

examples.flat: I'm a great cook, trust me.
examples.better: My sister refuses to come over unless I make the risotto. You can judge for yourself.
examples.note: A light, real endorsement is more convincing than a claim about yourself.

examples.flat: u should watch it
examples.better: literally everyone at work is obsessed with that show, i've held out two weeks, watch with me?
examples.note: Shared popularity plus an invitation makes it easy to say yes.

mistakes: Using negative social proof ('Everyone litters here') that normalises the bad behaviour.
Citing a group the listener doesn't identify with.
Making up or inflating numbers and reviews.
Using 'everyone's doing it' to pressure someone past their own judgement.

drills.prompt: Rewrite to use positive social proof: 'Too many people are skipping the safety training.'
models: Most of the floor has completed safety training already. Your slot is Tuesday at 10.
Nine out of ten people in your team have done it. It's 30 minutes.

drills.prompt: You want a hesitant client to try your service. Write a line using social proof honestly.
models: Two firms in your sector started with the same pilot. I can share how it went for them.
Our last three clients your size started small too. Here's what happened.

quiz.scenario: You want neighbours to recycle more. Which message works best?
options: Recycling rates here are terrible.
Most households on this street recycle every week.
Recycling saves the planet.
You'll be fined if you don't.
quiz.why: A positive descriptive norm from close neighbours is the strongest of the four.

quiz.scenario: Which social proof is most persuasive to a nurse considering a new scheduling app?
options: A celebrity endorsement
A count of total downloads worldwide
A testimonial from nurses at a similar hospital
A review from a software engineer
quiz.why: The closer the comparison group to the listener, the stronger the effect.

techniques.ethics: Pointing to what similar people really do is fair; faking reviews, inflating numbers or pressuring someone with 'everyone else' is not.

techniques.name: Credibility and Liking
techniques.aka: Ethos, authority, similarity, warmth plus competence
sources: Burger et al., What a coincidence! (2004)
techniques.summary: People say yes to those they trust and like: show real competence, real care, and real common ground.
techniques.why: Aristotle argued that the speaker's character (ethos) is one of the strongest proofs, and modern research agrees: we follow credible experts and say yes more to people we like. Even small genuine similarities, like a shared birthday in one study, raised compliance. Credibility is strongest when competence comes with warmth and a willingness to admit limits.
steps: Let your track record show briefly and specifically, without bragging.
Admit one small weakness or limit; it makes the rest more believable.
Look for genuine common ground early and mention it.
Show warmth: attention, a smile, interest in their goals.
Give honest compliments that are specific.

examples.flat: Trust me, I know what I'm doing.
examples.better: I ran this same rollout at my last company. We hit two snags; here's how I'd avoid them.
examples.note: Specific experience plus admitted snags builds more credibility than a claim.

examples.flat: We're the best in the market.
examples.better: We're not the cheapest. We are the ones with the lowest failure rate in your industry.
examples.note: Conceding a weakness makes the strength more believable.

examples.flat: I like travelling too.
examples.better: Wait, you did the night train to Vienna? I did that in a snowstorm. Which carriage were you in?
examples.note: A specific shared experience creates instant connection.

examples.flat: You're beautiful.
examples.better: You were brilliant tonight with my dad. And you look unreal in that.
examples.note: Specific, observed praise reads as true, which is what makes it land.

examples.flat: I'm sure this will work.
examples.better: I'd put it at 70% this works. If it doesn't, here's our fallback.
examples.note: Honest calibration signals expertise and earns trust for later.

examples.flat: You should listen to me, I've been there.
examples.better: I went through almost the same thing in 2019. Want to hear what I wish I'd done?
examples.note: Offers relevant experience as an option, not a lecture.

examples.flat: Because I'm your father.
examples.better: I made exactly this mistake at your age. I'll tell you how it went, then it's your call.
examples.note: Credibility from experience persuades teens; authority by title rarely does.

examples.flat: we have so much in common
examples.better: ok you also hate coriander? this might actually work
examples.note: Playful recognition of a real similarity builds liking without overclaiming.

mistakes: Name-dropping and bragging, which lowers liking.
Faking similarities or interests you don't have.
Flattery that is generic or obviously strategic.
Claiming expertise outside your real area.

drills.prompt: You're new and need a senior team to accept your proposal. Write an opener that builds ethos honestly.
models: I've only been here a month, so tell me what I'm missing. At my last job I cut onboarding time by half, and I think a version of that works here.
Before the idea: you know this system better than I do. I've solved a similar problem twice.

drills.prompt: Turn a generic compliment to your partner into a specific one: 'You're great.'
models: The way you handled that call with your sister was so calm. I was impressed.
You're the only person who can make me laugh when I'm this tired.

quiz.scenario: Which line builds the most credibility with a sceptical buyer?
options: We're the best, period.
We're not the cheapest, but our uptime has been 99.9% for five years.
Everyone loves us.
I personally guarantee you'll be thrilled.
quiz.why: Admitting a weakness and giving a specific, checkable strength earns trust.

quiz.scenario: You meet someone at a wedding. Which approach builds liking fastest?
options: Talk about your achievements
Agree with everything they say
Compliment them on everything
Find a genuine shared connection and ask about it
quiz.why: Real similarity plus curiosity builds liking; fake agreement and flattery feel hollow.

techniques.ethics: Showing real competence and real warmth is fair; faking credentials, inventing common ground or love-bombing to lower someone's guard is manipulation.

techniques.name: Scarcity, Honestly Framed
sources: Worchel, Lee & Adewole, Effects of supply and demand on ratings of object value (1975)
techniques.summary: Point out what's genuinely limited or unique, and when a real window closes, so people can decide in time.
techniques.why: We value things more when they are rare or slipping away; in a classic study, cookies from a nearly empty jar were rated more desirable than identical ones from a full jar. Honest scarcity helps people prioritise by telling them what's true about timing and uniqueness. Fake scarcity works briefly and then destroys trust.
steps: Find what is truly limited: time, places, your availability, something unique.
State it plainly and specifically, without hype.
Explain what they'd miss, not just that it's rare.
Give a real deadline and stick to it.
Never invent a limit.

examples.flat: Buy now, prices are going up soon!
examples.better: This rate is fixed until 30 June, when our new pricing starts. After that it's 12% higher.
examples.note: A specific, true deadline helps them plan rather than feel pressured.

examples.flat: Can we please get this approved?
examples.better: The vendor holds our slot until Friday. After that, the next opening is September.
examples.note: Explaining the real cost of waiting gets the decision made.

examples.flat: We should go away sometime.
examples.better: The cherry blossoms in Kyoto last about ten days. I want to see them with you this spring.
examples.note: Natural scarcity makes the plan feel special and urgent in a romantic way.

examples.flat: I'm free whenever you are.
examples.better: I'm away next week, but I'd love to see you Thursday before I go.
examples.note: Honest, limited availability creates a natural reason to commit to a date.

examples.flat: Come to the gig!
examples.better: It's their last show before they split. I've got one spare ticket and I want you there.
examples.note: Genuine uniqueness plus a personal invitation.

examples.flat: Visit more!
examples.better: Grandad's turning 90 once. Can we get everyone to Sunday lunch on the 12th?
examples.note: A one-time milestone motivates more than a general plea.

examples.flat: free this weekend?
examples.better: the market's only on this weekend, want to go saturday?
examples.note: A small real constraint gives an easy reason to decide now.

examples.flat: Spots are filling up fast!!! Don't miss out!!!
examples.better: We have 12 places on the course. 8 are taken.
examples.note: Plain numbers are more credible than shouting about scarcity.

mistakes: Inventing deadlines or 'only two left' claims.
Using hype words that make you sound like a pushy ad.
Playing hard to get by pretending to be busy.
Pressuring someone to decide before they can think.

drills.prompt: Rewrite honestly: 'Last chance!!! This offer won't last!!!'
models: The early-bird price ends Friday at midnight. After that it's the standard rate.
We're taking 10 clients this quarter. Six slots are left.

drills.prompt: You want your partner to plan a date with you. Use real scarcity, playfully.
models: My mum has the kids Saturday. That's a whole evening. What are we doing with it?
We have one child-free night this month. I have ideas. Do you?

quiz.scenario: Which use of scarcity is ethical?
options: Saying 'only 2 left' when you have 200
Pretending another buyer is interested
Mentioning a real price rise on a real date
Telling them the offer expires in an hour that you'll extend anyway
quiz.why: Honest scarcity gives true information about timing; the others are lies.

quiz.scenario: You like someone and you're both free a lot. What's the best approach?
options: Be warm and propose a specific plan
Pretend you're busy to seem in demand
Wait three days to reply
Cancel once to show you have options
quiz.why: Fake scarcity in dating backfires; clear interest and a concrete plan work better.

techniques.ethics: Telling people the truth about deadlines and limits is fair; fake countdowns, invented rival buyers and playing hard to get are deception.

techniques.name: Framing, Contrast and Anchoring
techniques.aka: Gain vs loss frame, contrast principle, first number
sources: Tversky & Kahneman, The framing of decisions and the psychology of choice (1981)
Galinsky & Mussweiler, First offers as anchors (2001)
techniques.summary: Present the same facts in the light that fits the decision: as a gain or as an avoided loss, next to a meaningful comparison, and with a well-chosen first number.
techniques.why: People react differently to equivalent options depending on whether they're described as gains or losses, and losses tend to loom larger. Our judgements are pulled toward the first number we hear, which is why research finds that making the first offer often gives an advantage. Contrast does the same: things look bigger, cheaper or better depending on what sits next to them.
steps: Decide whether the listener is more motivated by gaining something or not losing something.
Choose a fair comparison point that makes the value clear.
In negotiation, consider making a bold but defensible first offer.
Give a reason for your anchor so it's credible.
Keep the facts true; only the emphasis changes.

examples.flat: This tool costs 6,000 a year.
examples.better: This tool costs about 500 a month, and it replaces 20 hours of manual work.
examples.note: Breaking the cost down and contrasting it with time saved reframes the price.

examples.flat: What salary are you thinking?
examples.better: Based on market data for this role, I'm looking at 85 to 90.
examples.note: A researched, well-reasoned first number anchors the conversation in your range.

examples.flat: If we do this, we'll gain some efficiency.
examples.better: Right now we're losing about two days a month to this bug.
examples.note: Loss framing often motivates action more than the same gain.

examples.flat: Should we go out or stay in?
examples.better: We could do another night of laptops on the sofa, or dinner and that bar with the jazz. Your call.
examples.note: Contrast makes the more romantic option shine, while leaving her the choice.

examples.flat: Can you please exercise more?
examples.better: Twenty minutes of walking a day and you keep up with the grandkids for years.
examples.note: A gain frame tied to what he loves beats a lecture about health risks.

examples.flat: I'm not that interesting.
examples.better: Fair warning: my best story involves a goat and a wedding. Your bar is set very low.
examples.note: Playfully lowering the anchor makes anything you share feel like a win.

examples.flat: It's 300 for the weekend.
examples.better: It's 300 for the weekend, less than a night out each night, and we get a lake.
examples.note: Contrasting with a familiar cost makes the price feel reasonable.

examples.flat: We were hoping for around 30k, maybe less.
examples.better: Projects of this scope typically run 35 to 40. Here's what's included.
examples.note: A reasoned anchor beats an apologetic one, which invites a lowball.

mistakes: Using a frame that hides important facts.
Throwing out an extreme anchor with no reason, which can end the conversation.
Contrasting with a fake 'original price' that never existed.
Using loss framing to create fear that isn't warranted.

drills.prompt: Reframe as an avoided loss: 'If you renew now, you'll get the loyalty discount.'
models: If you don't renew by Friday, you'll lose the loyalty discount you've built up.
Waiting means giving up the 15% you've earned.

drills.prompt: You're freelancing and asked for a quote. Write a first-offer line with an anchor and a reason.
models: For a site with this many pages and integrations, it's typically 8 to 10k. I can walk you through it.
Based on the scope, I'd quote 9,500. That includes two rounds of revisions.

quiz.scenario: You're negotiating a salary and know the market range is 70 to 85. What's usually your strongest move?
options: Wait for them to name a number
Ask for 60 to be safe
Anchor near the top with your reasoning
Say 'whatever is fair'
quiz.why: A well-reasoned first offer tends to anchor the outcome; lowballing yourself sets a low ceiling.

quiz.scenario: Which frame best motivates a team to fix a slow process?
options: It would be nice to be a bit faster.
We could gain some efficiency.
Speed is important.
We lose a full day every week to this.
quiz.why: A concrete loss is more motivating than a vague gain.

techniques.ethics: Choosing honest emphasis and fair comparisons is persuasion; fake reference prices, hidden facts or manufactured fear are deception.

techniques.name: The 'Because' Reason
techniques.aka: Giving a reason, the copy machine effect
sources: Langer, Blank & Chanowitz, The mindlessness of ostensibly thoughtful action (1978)
techniques.summary: Attach a short, real reason to your request so it feels fair rather than arbitrary.
techniques.why: In a classic study, people asking to cut a copier queue got more yeses when they added a reason, even a weak one, for small favours; for bigger favours only a real reason helped. Replications are mixed, so treat it as 'reasons help' rather than a magic word. A reason shows respect and lets people judge the request on its merits.
steps: Make your request clear and short.
Add 'because' and the real reason.
Keep the reason relevant to them where you can.
For bigger asks, make the reason stronger and more specific.
Don't invent reasons.

examples.flat: Can you send it today?
examples.better: Can you send it today, because the client presents tomorrow morning?
examples.note: A real reason makes the urgency understandable, not bossy.

examples.flat: Can we pay in 60 days?
examples.better: Can we pay in 60 days, because our funding lands at the end of next month?
examples.note: A concrete reason makes the request sound reasonable and planned.

examples.flat: Put your phone away.
examples.better: Phones away tonight, because I want you all to myself.
examples.note: The reason turns a rule into a compliment and an invitation.

examples.flat: Go to bed.
examples.better: Bed now, because we're leaving early for the beach.
examples.note: A reason tied to something fun gets less pushback.

examples.flat: Can we move dinner to 8?
examples.better: Can we move dinner to 8, because I want to come from the gym without rushing?
examples.note: Explaining your need gets a quicker, easier yes.

examples.flat: Want to get coffee?
examples.better: I want to take you to this tiny coffee place, because you said you're a snob about espresso.
examples.note: A reason that shows you listened turns an invite into something personal.

examples.flat: Please use the new template.
examples.better: Please use the new template, because it auto-fills the client data and saves you ten minutes.
examples.note: A reason that benefits them is the most persuasive kind.

examples.flat: call me
examples.better: call me when you can, because I have news and it's good
examples.note: A reason, and a reassuring one, gets a quick call back.

mistakes: Giving a fake or empty reason as a trick.
Writing long justifications that sound defensive.
Relying on 'because' for big asks without a real argument.
Giving a reason that's only about you when you could link it to them.

drills.prompt: Add a good reason: 'Can I leave early on Friday?'
models: Can I leave at three on Friday, because my sister's flight lands at four? I'll finish the report Thursday.
Could I head off early Friday, because I've got the move? Everything on my list will be done.

drills.prompt: Add a playful reason to an invite: 'Come to bed.'
models: Come to bed, because it's cold and you're warm.
Come to bed, because I've been waiting all day to have you to myself.

quiz.scenario: What does the evidence best support about the word 'because'?
options: It works like a magic word for any request
Real reasons help, especially for small asks; for bigger asks the reason must be good
It never makes a difference
It only works in writing
quiz.why: The original study found weak reasons only helped small favours, and replications are mixed.

quiz.scenario: Which request is best?
options: Can you cover my shift, because it's important?
Cover my shift.
Can you cover my shift? I'd really owe you, please please please.
Can you cover my shift Saturday, because it's my brother's wedding? I'll take your Sunday.
quiz.why: Specific reason plus a fair offer in return; the others are vague or pleading.

techniques.ethics: Giving the real reason respects people's judgement; inventing reasons to slip a request past them is deception.

techniques.name: Autonomy: 'But You Are Free' and Two Yeses
techniques.aka: BYAF, alternative choice, the illusion-free choice
sources: Guéguen & Pascual, Evocation of freedom and compliance (2000)
Carpenter, A meta-analysis of the effectiveness of the 'but you are free' compliance-gaining technique (2013)
Brehm, A Theory of Psychological Reactance (1966)
techniques.summary: Remind people that the choice is theirs, and where it fits, offer two options you're both happy with instead of a yes/no.
techniques.why: Pressure triggers reactance: people push back to defend their freedom. Saying 'but of course it's up to you' lowers that pushback, and a meta-analysis found a reliable boost in compliance on average, though stricter re-analyses suggest the effect is smaller than first thought. Offering two good options keeps the person in control while moving things forward.
steps: Make your request or suggestion clearly.
Add a genuine freedom line: 'but it's totally your call'.
Where possible, offer two specific options you'd be glad with.
Make 'neither' a real option too.
Respect the answer, including no.

examples.flat: You need to take the training.
examples.better: I think the training would really help with the new system, but it's your call.
examples.note: Removing pressure makes people more open, not less.

examples.flat: Sign now or the deal's off.
examples.better: Take a look over the weekend. If it's not right for you, no hard feelings.
examples.note: Granting space reduces reactance and builds trust for the yes.

examples.flat: Want to go out with me?
examples.better: I'd love to take you out. Drinks Thursday or a walk Sunday morning? Or tell me I'm out of luck.
examples.note: Two easy options plus a graceful out make yes easy and no comfortable.

examples.flat: Let's go to bed.
examples.better: Movie on the sofa, or an early night with me? (smile) Dealer's choice.
examples.note: A playful choice of two keeps it flirtatious and fully hers.

examples.flat: Put your coat on now!
examples.better: Red coat or blue coat today?
examples.note: Two acceptable options give a child control and avoid the power struggle.

examples.flat: You have to come to my party.
examples.better: I'd love you at the party Saturday. No pressure though, I know you've had a week.
examples.note: A real out makes friends more likely to come, not less.

examples.flat: Can you take on this project?
examples.better: Would you rather lead the dashboard or the API piece? Or if neither fits right now, say so.
examples.note: A choice gets engagement while still respecting capacity.

examples.flat: come over?
examples.better: come over tonight, or I come to you? either way I'm bringing dessert. (no worries if you're wiped)
examples.note: Options plus a real out reads as confident and considerate.

mistakes: Saying 'it's your choice' with a tone that clearly means it isn't.
Offering a 'choice' between two things they don't want.
Using the two-option close to steamroll a clear no.
Overusing the phrase until it sounds like a script.

drills.prompt: Rewrite with autonomy language: 'You should really see a doctor about that.'
models: I'd feel better if a doctor took a look. But you know your body, it's up to you.
Would you rather I book something or would you like to do it? Or we wait a week and see?

drills.prompt: Invite your partner to try something new together (e.g. a dance class) using a choice of two and a real out.
models: Tuesday beginner class or Saturday's? Or if it sounds awful, tell me and I'll find something else.
Salsa or swing? I'm in for either, and I'll drop it if you're not into it.

quiz.scenario: A friend is hesitant to lend you a car. Which line uses 'but you are free' honestly?
options: You're free to say no, but you'd be letting me down.
It's your choice, so just say yes.
Would it be possible to borrow it Saturday? Totally fine if not.
Everyone else would lend it.
quiz.why: A genuine out with no hidden guilt is the whole point.

quiz.scenario: What's the problem with 'Do you want to sign today or tomorrow?' when the person hasn't decided to buy at all?
options: It's a false choice that ignores their real option of no
It's too polite
It uses social proof
Nothing, it's ideal
quiz.why: Two yeses are fair only when they've already shown interest and 'no' is still on the table.

techniques.ethics: Real choice and a real out are fair; a fake choice that hides 'no', or 'it's up to you' said with guilt attached, is manipulation.

techniques.name: Story and the Memorable Line
techniques.aka: Narrative, rule of three, antithesis, rhetorical figures
sources: Green & Brock, The role of transportation in the persuasiveness of public narratives (2000)
Small, Loewenstein & Slovic, Sympathy and callousness (2007)
Shu & Carlson, When three charms but four alarms (2014)
techniques.summary: Persuade with one vivid person or moment rather than a pile of statistics, and package your key point in a shape people remember: three beats, a contrast, a short closing line.
techniques.why: When people get absorbed in a story, they argue back less and remember more, and research shows one identifiable person moves us more than large numbers. Three claims tend to persuade better than two or four, because more starts to feel like overselling. Figures like antithesis ('not this, but that') and rhythm make a line easy to recall and repeat.
steps: Find one real person or moment that shows your point.
Tell it briefly: situation, problem, turning point, result.
Then give the number, if you have one, as support.
Distil the point into three beats or a contrast.
End with a short line you'd want repeated.

examples.flat: Our users are frustrated with onboarding, satisfaction is down 12%.
examples.better: Last week a nurse called us at 2am in tears because she couldn't log a patient in. That's our onboarding.
examples.note: A single vivid person makes the number impossible to ignore.

examples.flat: We're reliable, fast and affordable and flexible and experienced.
examples.better: Three things: we ship on time, we pick up the phone, and we fix it if we're wrong.
examples.note: Three concrete claims land; five generic ones sound like a brochure.

examples.flat: I love you a lot.
examples.better: I didn't fall for you on our first date. I fell for you the night you fixed the boiler in my coat.
examples.note: A specific memory with a contrast is far more moving than a general statement.

examples.flat: I'm adventurous.
examples.better: I once took a wrong bus in Sicily and ended up at a stranger's olive harvest. Stayed three days.
examples.note: A short story shows a trait instead of claiming it.

examples.flat: We should prioritise quality.
examples.better: We don't need more features. We need fewer that work.
examples.note: Antithesis gives the team a line they'll repeat in meetings.

examples.flat: You should save money.
examples.better: Your grandmother saved a little every Friday for forty years. It bought this house.
examples.note: A family story persuades where advice bounces off.

examples.flat: You should come, it'll be fun.
examples.better: Good food, old friends, no phones. Saturday.
examples.note: Three short beats make the invitation feel complete and easy to remember.

examples.flat: had a good time tonight
examples.better: came for the dinner. stayed for the company. leaving with your scarf, apparently.
examples.note: Rhythm plus a playful twist makes the message memorable and flirty.

mistakes: Telling long stories with no point or no pay-off.
Inventing stories and presenting them as true.
Stuffing in too many claims, which triggers scepticism.
Using slogans with nothing behind them.

drills.prompt: Turn into a story-led point: 'Our app saves people time.'
models: Maria, a teacher, used to spend Sundays on lesson plans. Now she's done by Friday lunch. That's what this does.
One customer told us he got his Sunday back. That's the whole pitch.

drills.prompt: Write a closing line for a toast at a friend's wedding using antithesis or a rule of three.
models: He's not the man who never falls. He's the man who always gets back up, and now he has someone to catch him.
To laughter, to patience, and to never going to bed angry.

quiz.scenario: You want donations for a food bank. Which appeal is likely to work best?
options: Statistics on regional hunger
A list of ten reasons to give
A short story about one family who used the food bank
A chart of rising food prices
quiz.why: One identifiable person tends to move people more than numbers, which can be added after.

quiz.scenario: How many claims should you lead with in a pitch to avoid seeming like you're overselling?
options: Three
One
Five
As many as possible
quiz.why: Research found three claims persuade best; four or more trigger scepticism.

techniques.ethics: True stories and memorable framing are fair; invented anecdotes or emotional stories that hide relevant facts are manipulation.

modules.title: Leading the Conversation
modules.tagline: Steer where the talk goes without grabbing the wheel.
modules.intro: These techniques decide what a conversation is about and where it ends up: setting the frame, reframing, asking the right questions and staying steady when it gets heated. Use them in meetings, negotiations, family talks and on dates, any time you want the conversation to go somewhere good for both of you.

techniques.name: Set the Frame Early
sources: Galinsky & Mussweiler, First offers as anchors (2001)
techniques.summary: Decide what a conversation is about and what it is for, and say so before the details arrive.
techniques.why: The first purpose, number or mood on the table becomes the anchor everything after it is measured against. Research on negotiation finds that whoever makes the first reasonable offer tends to pull the final deal toward it. Naming the frame early also removes guesswork, so people relax and follow your lead.
steps: Decide the one thing this conversation is for.
Say it in the first thirty seconds, in one sentence.
Name what a good outcome looks like.
If numbers matter, put a well justified one on the table first.
When things drift, point back to the frame.

examples.flat: So, um, I had a few thoughts about the project, but whatever you think.
examples.better: I want ten minutes to pick one of two options, and leave with a decision.
examples.note: Naming purpose, time and outcome stops the meeting from sprawling.

examples.flat: So what's your budget?
examples.better: Projects like this usually land between 18 and 22 thousand. Let me show you what decides where yours falls.
examples.note: A justified range anchors the talk around your numbers.

examples.flat: Do you want to do something on Saturday?
examples.better: Saturday is ours. Phones away after six, and I've planned the first hour.
examples.note: Frames the evening as special before any details are known.

examples.flat: Want to grab a coffee sometime?
examples.better: I know a place with terrible coffee and the best pastries in town. Thursday?
examples.note: Frames the date as a small adventure, not an interview.

examples.flat: Can we talk about Christmas?
examples.better: I want us to plan Christmas so nobody ends up exhausted. Can we start there?
examples.note: Sets a shared goal before the logistics argument begins.

examples.flat: Sorry, I just need to vent.
examples.better: I need five minutes of venting, no advice, then I'm all yours.
examples.note: Tells them what role to play, so they don't jump in with fixes.

examples.flat: hey are you free tonight
examples.better: Tonight's plan: takeaway, that film you keep mentioning, and you stealing my blanket. In?
examples.note: Paints the frame so saying yes is easy and warm.

examples.flat: We need to talk.
examples.better: Nothing's wrong. I just want to talk about how we get more evenings like last Friday.
examples.note: Removes the dread and frames the talk as building, not fixing.

mistakes: Opening with apologies that frame you as a nuisance.
Anchoring with a number you can't justify.
Setting a frame, then dropping it the moment someone pushes.
Framing so tightly that nobody else gets a say.

drills.prompt: Rewrite this meeting opener: 'Hey, so, deadlines have been a bit off lately.'
models: I want us to leave with one change that gets us back on schedule. Let's look at where the last three slipped.
This is a fix it meeting, not a blame meeting. Twenty minutes, one plan.

drills.prompt: You've both had a rough week. Set the frame for tonight in one text to your partner.
models: Rough week. Tonight: no work talk, your full attention, and I'm bringing wine.
Tonight we're off duty. I cook, you pick the music, nobody mentions email.

quiz.scenario: You're asking your manager for a raise. Which opener sets the strongest frame?
options: Sorry to bother you, I know budgets are tight...
I'd like to talk about my pay. I've brought what I delivered this year and the market range for the role.
Do you think I might be due a raise at some point?
Other people have been getting raises, so...
quiz.why: It states the purpose and brings a yardstick, with no apology and no comparison to others.

quiz.scenario: A friend suggests 'a quick catch up', but you need help moving house. What's the best frame?
options: Say nothing and ask at the end
Hint about how heavy your sofa is
Text the request after you've left
Up front: 'I'd love to catch up, and I also want to ask a favour. Can I do that first?'
quiz.why: Naming the real purpose early is honest and lets them answer freely, instead of feeling ambushed later.

techniques.ethics: Fair when the frame is honest and others can push back; manipulative when you anchor with fake numbers or hide the real purpose.

techniques.name: Reframing
sources: Tversky & Kahneman, The framing of decisions and the psychology of choice (1981)
Brooks, Get excited: reappraising pre-performance anxiety as excitement (2014)
techniques.summary: Change what a situation means by showing it in a different light that is also true.
techniques.why: People react to the meaning they give facts, not the facts alone. The same outcome described as a gain or as a loss leads to different choices, and relabelling nerves as excitement improves performance in studies. A new, honest meaning can turn resistance into energy.
steps: Listen for the current frame: what does this mean to them?
Acknowledge the feeling first.
Find another meaning that is also true.
Offer it lightly, as an observation or a question.
Let them try it on; don't force it.

examples.flat: Yeah, the client rejected it again.
examples.better: The client just told us exactly what they don't want. Two options gone, one to go.
examples.note: Turns rejection into narrowing progress.

examples.flat: Don't be nervous, it's only a presentation.
examples.better: That buzz is your body getting ready. Call it excitement and use it.
examples.note: Echoes reappraisal research: anxiety and excitement feel alike in the body.

examples.flat: I suppose I could do a small discount.
examples.better: Fair. Let's look at it per month of use instead of one lump, and see if it still feels expensive.
examples.note: Changes the unit of comparison without changing the price.

examples.flat: You're not needy, stop saying that.
examples.better: You're not needy. You're telling me what matters to you, and I like knowing.
examples.note: Recasts a worry about herself as a strength.

examples.flat: Ugh, another quiet weekend at home.
examples.better: A whole weekend with nowhere to be and nobody to impress. I have ideas.
examples.note: Turns boredom into anticipation, with a playful hint.

examples.flat: Sorry I'm late, I'm the worst.
examples.better: Sorry I'm late. On the bright side, you got ten minutes to pick the best seat.
examples.note: Owns it, then lightens the frame instead of grovelling.

examples.flat: That sucks that you got dumped.
examples.better: That hurts. And you just got your Saturdays back. Want to fill the first one?
examples.note: Acknowledges the loss first, then opens a forward looking frame.

examples.flat: Mum, please stop worrying about me.
examples.better: Mum, I know worrying is how you love me. Can I show you why I'm OK?
examples.note: Reframes nagging as care, which lowers defences on both sides.

mistakes: Reframing before acknowledging the feeling, which comes across as toxic positivity.
Offering a frame that isn't actually true.
Pushing the new frame after they reject it.
Using reframes to dodge responsibility ('it's a learning opportunity').

drills.prompt: Reframe for a colleague: 'We lost the pitch, the whole quarter is wasted.'
models: Losing hurts. We also now have a finished deck and their feedback for the next three pitches.
We lost the result, not the work. What can we reuse?

drills.prompt: Your partner says: 'We never go out anymore.' Reframe and respond.
models: You're right, and I miss it too. Let's make this the start of a habit: Friday, my pick.
Sounds like you miss our adventures. Me too. Pick a date and I'll plan the rest.

quiz.scenario: A teammate groans: 'This bug ate my whole day.' Which line reframes best?
options: At least it's not the weekend.
You spent a day learning this system better than anyone. What did you find?
Bugs happen, move on.
You should have asked for help sooner.
quiz.why: It offers a true, more useful meaning and invites them to share, rather than dismissing or blaming.

quiz.scenario: Your partner is anxious about meeting your friends. Which response reframes well?
options: Don't be silly, it's fine.
They're not scary.
Just be yourself.
They're curious about the person I can't stop talking about. You walk in already liked.
quiz.why: It replaces 'being judged' with 'already welcome', which is true and calming.

techniques.ethics: Fair when the new meaning is true and they can reject it; manipulative when it hides a real cost or brushes off a real feeling.

techniques.name: Assumptive Language & Presuppositions
techniques.aka: Presupposition, the assumptive close, alternative choice
sources: Loftus & Palmer, Reconstruction of automobile destruction (1974)
techniques.summary: Phrase things so the outcome you expect is treated as given, and ask only about the details.
techniques.why: Words carry hidden assumptions that listeners often accept without checking; in a classic study, the verb used in a question changed how fast people remembered cars going. In daily talk, assuming the positive makes the comfortable path the default. Sales style 'cash or card' closes are less well supported, so keep the effect rating modest.
steps: Decide the outcome you honestly expect.
Ask about the how or the when, not the whether.
Keep a clear, easy exit open.
If they question the assumption, drop it gracefully.

examples.flat: Would you be able to review this at some point?
examples.better: When's good for you to review this, Tuesday or Wednesday?
examples.note: Assumes the review happens and asks only about timing.

examples.flat: Are you interested in going ahead?
examples.better: If you go ahead, which start date suits your team better, the 1st or the 15th?
examples.note: Moves the talk from whether to when, while leaving room to say neither.

examples.flat: Do you maybe want to see me again?
examples.better: Next time, I'm picking the restaurant.
examples.note: Playfully presumes a next time; easy to laugh off if not.

examples.flat: Are you going to be tired tonight?
examples.better: Save some energy for later. I have plans for you.
examples.note: Presumes the evening together and builds anticipation.

examples.flat: Do you want to go away for your birthday?
examples.better: Mountains or sea for your birthday?
examples.note: The trip is a given; the fun choice is hers.

examples.flat: Are you coming to the barbecue?
examples.better: What are you bringing to the barbecue?
examples.note: Treats them as already part of the plan.

examples.flat: Can you please tidy your room?
examples.better: Do you want to do your room before or after dinner?
examples.note: Gives a teenager real control over timing, not over whether.

examples.flat: Is it ok if I call you later?
examples.better: Calling you at 8 to hear how it went.
examples.note: Confident and warm, and they can easily say not tonight.

mistakes: Presuming something they've already said no to.
False choices that hide the real option, like 'cash or card' before they've agreed to buy.
Sounding like a sales script.
Getting rattled when they reject the premise.

drills.prompt: Rewrite with a presupposition: 'Would you be open to maybe having a call?'
models: What's better for a twenty minute call, Thursday or Friday?
