techniques.why: When people are absorbed in a story they argue against it less, an effect researchers call narrative transportation. A story also lets you raise a sensitive idea without pointing at the listener. The conclusion feels like theirs, so it sticks.
steps: Pick a short, true story that carries your point.
Keep it under a minute.
Include one vivid detail.
Don't spell out the moral; let it hang or ask what they make of it.

examples.flat: We need to test more before launch.
examples.better: Last job, we skipped testing to hit a date. Launch day, the checkout button didn't work. We hit the date and lost the month.
examples.note: Makes the cost vivid without a lecture.

examples.flat: Cheaper suppliers are risky.
examples.better: A client last year went with the cheapest quote. They called us in March to rebuild it. Lovely people, still a bit sore.
examples.note: Lets the buyer imagine the risk for themselves.

examples.flat: We should travel more.
examples.better: I keep thinking about that night in Porto when we got lost and found the tiny bar with the singer.
examples.note: Rekindles the feeling, so the suggestion makes itself.

examples.flat: I'm really adventurous.
examples.better: Last summer I signed up for a sailing course thinking it'd be relaxing. Day one, I fell in.
examples.note: Shows instead of tells, with some self mocking humour.

examples.flat: You should go to therapy.
examples.better: When I started seeing someone, I didn't think I needed it. Three sessions in, I was sleeping better.
examples.note: Shares your experience without pressure.

examples.flat: You need to wear a helmet.
examples.better: My mate came off his bike at ten miles an hour. The helmet split in two and he walked away fine.
examples.note: One concrete image beats a rule.

examples.flat: We should do something fun.
examples.better: Remember when we did karaoke and you did the whole of Bohemian Rhapsody? I think about it weekly.
examples.note: The memory invites a repeat.

mistakes: Rambling stories with no clear point.
Stories so obviously about them that they feel like a sermon.
Making stories up.
Explaining the moral at the end.

drills.prompt: Hint to a friend that they cancel plans too often, using a story.
models: My sister once told me that every time I cancelled, she felt like a backup plan. It changed how I do things.
I used to cancel on people loads. One friend just stopped inviting me, and it took me a year to notice why.

drills.prompt: Suggest a weekend away to your partner with a story, not a request.
models: I was remembering the cabin: rain on the roof, you reading by the fire. I want that again.
Saw a photo of us at the lake today. We looked so relaxed. I miss that version of us.

quiz.scenario: Which story hint best encourages a colleague to delegate?
options: You should delegate.
Delegation is a key leadership skill.
My old boss did everything herself and burnt out in a year. Her replacement delegated and the team doubled its output.
Stop micromanaging.
quiz.why: A short, concrete story lets them reach the conclusion without feeling lectured.

quiz.scenario: What weakens a story hint most?
options: A vivid detail
Ending with 'and the moral is, you should listen to me'
Keeping it short
Telling a true story
quiz.why: Spelling out the moral turns a story back into a lecture and invites resistance.

techniques.ethics: Fair when the story is true and relevant; manipulative when it's invented or used to scare.

techniques.name: Escalate from Indirect to Direct
sources: Pinker, Nowak & Lee, The logic of indirect speech (2008)
techniques.summary: Start with a light hint, read the response, and step up toward a clear statement while the signals stay warm.
techniques.why: Each step gives the other person a low cost chance to signal yes or no, so you never overshoot. Rising directness also builds anticipation, because the tension is paced instead of dumped. It ends with clarity, so nothing important stays a guess.
steps: Start with a light, deniable hint.
Read the response: warmth, play, or coolness?
If warm, go one step clearer.
If cool, hold or step back.
End with a clear, direct question when the signals are good.

examples.flat: Do you want to kiss me?
examples.better: First 'I'm really enjoying this.' Later 'You're trouble, you know that?' Then 'I'd like to kiss you.'
examples.note: Each step checks in before the clearest one.

examples.flat: Do you want to fool around?
examples.better: First 'You smell amazing.' Then a long, slow hug. Then, quietly, 'Come here.'
examples.note: Builds anticipation and leaves room for her signals.

examples.flat: Your performance isn't good enough.
examples.better: First 'How are you finding the workload?' Then 'I noticed two deadlines slipped.' Then 'I need these on time from now on.'
examples.note: Opens with curiosity and lands with clarity.

examples.flat: We need a discount.
examples.better: First 'Budget's tight this year.' Then 'We need some room on price.' Then 'At ten percent off, we sign today.'
examples.note: Gives them the chance to offer first.

examples.flat: You're drinking too much.
examples.better: First 'You doing ok lately?' Then 'I've noticed the weekends getting bigger.' Then 'I'm worried about you.'
examples.note: A gentle way in, with an honest landing.

examples.flat: You can't stay with us for a month.
examples.better: First 'It'll be cosy with four of us!' Then 'We both work from home, so it'll be tight.' Then 'A week is our limit.'
examples.note: Escalates to a clear boundary.

examples.flat: Do you like me?
examples.better: First 'Tonight was fun.' Then 'I've been smiling all day.' Then 'I'd like to see you again, soon.'
examples.note: Rises with their replies.

mistakes: Staying in hint mode forever.
Jumping straight from a hint to a full declaration.
Ignoring a cool response and escalating anyway.
Escalating so slowly they think you're not interested.

drills.prompt: Plan a three step ladder to ask a colleague to stop interrupting you.
models: 1: 'Let me finish this thought.' 2: 'I've noticed I get cut off in these meetings.' 3: 'I need you to let me finish, then I'll hear you out.'
1: 'Hang on, nearly done.' 2: 'Can I finish? It happens a lot.' 3: 'Please stop interrupting me in meetings.'

drills.prompt: Write a three text ladder suggesting a date night to your partner.
models: 1: 'Thinking about you.' 2: 'Thinking about you in that green dress.' 3: 'Friday, eight, the green dress. I'm booking the table.'
1: 'Long day, missed you.' 2: 'I want you to myself this week.' 3: 'Thursday night is ours. Don't make plans.'

quiz.scenario: At step two of your ladder, they go quiet and change the subject. What next?
options: Hold or step back, and try again later only if the signals warm up
Go to step three immediately
Ask why they're being weird
Repeat step two louder
quiz.why: A cool response is information; the ladder only works if you respect it.

quiz.scenario: What's the main benefit of escalating gradually?
options: You never have to be direct
It confuses them into agreeing
It sounds more formal
Each step lets them signal yes or no at low cost
quiz.why: Pacing keeps both of you comfortable and makes the final direct step well judged.

techniques.ethics: Fair when each step responds to their signals; manipulative when small steps are used to wear down a no.

techniques.name: Choose Direct or Indirect: Read the Room
techniques.aka: High and low context, register switching
sources: Tannen, That's Not What I Meant! (1986)
techniques.summary: Pick how plainly to speak based on the person, the stakes, the culture and the moment.
techniques.why: People differ in how much they say outright versus imply, often shaped by culture and family. The same line can feel refreshingly honest to one person and rude to another, so matching their style helps the message land. Some things, like consent, deadlines and safety, always need plain words.
steps: Ask: how high are the stakes, and how close are we?
Notice how they talk: plain or layered?
Default to direct for requests, deadlines and consent.
Use indirect for play, early flirting and saving face.
Match them, then adjust if they misread you.

examples.flat: This is wrong. (said to a junior, in front of the team)
examples.better: In private: 'The numbers in section two don't add up. Can you recheck them before Thursday?'
examples.note: Direct content, private delivery, so they keep face.

examples.flat: Maybe someone could possibly look at the server?
examples.better: Ana, restart the server now. I'll update the client.
examples.note: In a crisis, clarity beats politeness.

examples.flat: We need you to lower the price.
examples.better: We're excited to work together. Our budget is a little below this, and we'd like to find a way.
examples.note: With a relationship first counterpart, a softer frame keeps doors open.

examples.flat: So are we exclusive or what? (on date two)
examples.better: I'm really enjoying getting to know you.
examples.note: Early on, indirect warmth fits; the direct talk comes later.

examples.flat: It's fine, you don't have to get me anything.
examples.better: I'd love flowers sometime. It makes me feel thought of.
examples.note: With a partner, direct is often kinder than a hint.

examples.flat: I want you. (texted while she's in a work meeting)
examples.better: Thinking about you. Tonight.
examples.note: The setting calls for subtext, and the meaning still lands.

examples.flat: You raised me badly.
examples.better: I'd like to talk about some things from growing up. Is now an ok time?
examples.note: High stakes call for direct but gentle, with permission.

examples.flat: You owe me two hundred. (in front of others)
examples.better: Later, alone: 'Hey, can you send the two hundred this week?'
examples.note: A direct ask in the right setting.

mistakes: Using one style with everyone.
Hinting about important needs, then resenting people for missing them.
Being blunt and calling it honesty.
Being indirect about consent: always be direct there.

drills.prompt: Your boss is very direct. You hinted that you're overloaded and nothing changed. Rewrite your message.
models: I can deliver two of these three by Friday. Which one should slip?
I'm at capacity. If the new project comes in, the report has to move.

drills.prompt: A new colleague from a culture that values indirectness made an error in a shared document. Message them.
models: Thanks for this! I wonder if the dates in row four might need another look. I could be wrong.
Great start. I noticed something small in row four. Shall we look at it together?

quiz.scenario: When should you always be direct?
options: Early flirting
Teasing a partner
Asking for consent
Hinting at a birthday gift
quiz.why: Consent needs a clear question and a clear answer; subtext isn't enough.

quiz.scenario: A colleague says 'That's an interesting approach' and pauses. What's most likely?
options: They love it
They may have reservations, so ask what they'd change
They didn't hear you
They want to take it over
quiz.why: Many indirect speakers signal doubt this way; a curious question brings it into the open.

techniques.ethics: Fair when you adapt so you're understood; manipulative when you go vague to dodge accountability or blunt to dominate.

techniques.name: Say the Quiet Part Kindly
techniques.aka: Radical candour, naming the elephant, softened start-up
sources: Gottman, The Seven Principles for Making Marriage Work (1999)
techniques.summary: Name the uncomfortable truth everyone is avoiding, with care, so the conversation can actually move.
techniques.why: Unspoken issues leak out as tension, sarcasm and distance. Gottman's research found that the way a hard conversation starts strongly predicts how it ends, so a soft, clear opening makes progress far more likely. Caring and being candid at the same time is what makes the truth hearable.
steps: Notice what isn't being said.
Start soft: share your feeling and your good intent first.
Name the thing in one clear sentence.
Own your part.
Invite their view and listen.

examples.flat: Everything's fine between us.
examples.better: Can I say the awkward thing? I think we both want the lead role, and it's making us weird with each other.
examples.note: Naming the hidden competition takes the charge out of it.

examples.flat: Let's keep going and see.
examples.better: I think we're both worried about looking like we lost. Can we find a version where neither of us does?
examples.note: Names the face saving issue so you can solve it.

examples.flat: Nothing's wrong.
examples.better: I've noticed we haven't been close in a while. I miss you, and I don't want us to drift.
examples.note: Soft start, clear truth, shared goal.

examples.flat: You're never in the mood.
examples.better: I want you, and I feel a bit shy saying it. Can we talk about what helps you feel like it?
examples.note: Vulnerable and kind instead of blaming.

examples.flat: Haha, yeah, sure. (when a friend keeps joking about your job)
examples.better: I know you mean it as a joke, but the jokes about my job are starting to sting.
examples.note: Kind, specific and honest.

examples.flat: It's fine, I'll host again.
examples.better: I love having everyone, and I'm exhausted. Can someone else host next year?
examples.note: Truth with love, plus a clear ask.

examples.flat: Cool, see you sometime.
examples.better: I like you, and I'm not looking for anything serious right now. I'd rather say that early.
examples.note: Honest framing respects their time and choice.

examples.flat: k
examples.better: Honestly, that hurt a bit. Can we talk tonight?
examples.note: Names the feeling instead of sulking.

mistakes: Opening with criticism of their character.
Saying it in front of other people.
Unloading a whole list of grievances at once.
Saying it and leaving no room for their reply.

drills.prompt: Your flatmate never cleans. Say the quiet part kindly.
models: I like living with you, and I'm starting to feel resentful about the kitchen. Can we set up a rota?
Awkward thing: I'm doing most of the cleaning and it's bugging me. Can we fix it before it becomes a thing?

drills.prompt: Your partner has seemed distant since your argument last week. Open the conversation.
models: I think we're both still a bit hurt from last week. I'd like to clear it. Can we?
It feels like there's a little wall between us since Tuesday. I miss you. Can we talk?

quiz.scenario: Which is the best soft start-up?
options: You always ignore me.
Why are you like this?
I've been feeling lonely in the evenings and I'd love more time with you.
Whatever, it's fine.
quiz.why: It shares a feeling and a positive need, with no blame, so it invites closeness.

quiz.scenario: What does Gottman's research suggest about hard conversations between partners?
options: How they start strongly predicts how they end
They're best avoided
Criticism helps clear the air
Only the ending matters
quiz.why: A harsh start-up tends to end badly; a soft one gives the talk a real chance.

techniques.ethics: Fair when truth comes with care and their reply matters; harmful when 'just being honest' is cover for cruelty.

modules.title: Texting & Written Words
modules.tagline: Say more with fewer words on a screen.
modules.intro: Text strips away your voice, face and timing, so every word does more work. This module covers brevity, exits, callbacks, when to switch to voice, rhythm and invitations that actually turn into plans. Use it for flirting with a partner, messaging colleagues and keeping friendships alive between meetings.

techniques.name: Brevity & White Space
techniques.aka: Less is more, the short message
sources: Strunk & White, The Elements of Style (1959)
Kruger et al., Egocentrism Over E-mail (2005)
techniques.summary: Cut each message to the one line that matters and let the gap around it carry tone.
techniques.why: Short messages are easier to read, quicker to answer and leave room for the other person. Long blocks feel like homework and blur your point. Research on email shows people overestimate how clearly their tone comes across, so fewer, clearer words are safer than long, nuanced ones.
steps: Write the message, then delete the first sentence (it is usually warm-up).
Keep one idea per message.
Cut hedges like "just", "sorry to bother" and "I was wondering if maybe".
Read it aloud; if you wouldn't say it that way, rewrite it.

examples.flat: Hey, so I was just thinking about you and wanted to say I hope your day is going okay and that I'm looking forward to seeing you later on tonight if you're still free.
examples.better: Can't stop thinking about tonight.
examples.note: Five words carry more feeling than a paragraph of hedges.

examples.flat: I really really miss you so much and I can't wait for you to come home, it's been such a long week.
examples.better: Come home.
examples.note: Two words, with the space around them, say everything.

examples.flat: Haha yes that was so funny, I can't believe that happened, honestly I was laughing for ages.
examples.better: Still laughing.
examples.note: Brevity makes the reaction feel more genuine, not less.

examples.flat: Hi, I hope you're well! Just wanted to check in and see if you had a chance to look at the report I sent over last week?
examples.better: Any thoughts on the report? A yes or no on section 3 is enough for now.
examples.note: A short, specific ask is easier to answer.

examples.flat: I'm sorry but I think maybe we would probably need a slightly better price to make this work for us.
examples.better: We need 12 percent off to sign this week.
examples.note: Clear, short terms signal confidence.

examples.flat: Hey! Long time no talk, how are you, how's work, how's the family, how was the trip?
examples.better: Saw a dog that looked exactly like Bruno. Thought of you. How are you?
examples.note: One specific detail beats a list of questions.

examples.flat: Hi! I had such a great time on Saturday, I hope you did too, it was really nice to meet you and I'd love to do it again sometime if you're up for it.
examples.better: Saturday was great. Round two?
examples.note: Short and confident reads as relaxed interest.

mistakes: Being so brief you sound cold or annoyed ("k.").
Splitting one thought into ten rapid messages.
Cutting the context people actually need at work.
Using one-word replies to someone who is opening up.

drills.prompt: Cut to under eight words: "I just wanted to let you know that I'm really looking forward to seeing you tonight."
models: Counting the hours till tonight.
Tonight can't come soon enough.

drills.prompt: Rewrite for a colleague: "Sorry to bother you, I was just wondering if you might possibly have time to look at this?"
models: Could you review this by Thursday? Ten minutes, max.
Quick review needed on page 2. Free this afternoon?

drills.prompt: Reply to your partner's "Long day. Miss you." in five words or fewer.
models: Come here. I've got you.
Kettle's on. So am I.

quiz.scenario: Which message best uses brevity to flirt with a partner?
options: I've been thinking about you a lot today and I really hope you're having a nice time at work.
k
Distracted. Entirely your fault.
Hope you're well, let me know how your day is going.
quiz.why: It is short, playful and carries feeling without hedges or coldness.

quiz.scenario: When is brevity a mistake?
options: When your friend is sharing something painful and needs a fuller reply.
When you're confirming a time.
When you're flirting.
When you're asking a quick yes or no.
quiz.why: Brevity serves clarity; when someone opens up, a short reply can read as dismissive.

techniques.ethics: Be brief to respect attention, not to withhold warmth or keep someone guessing on purpose.

techniques.name: Ending on a High
techniques.aka: Leave before the peak, the clean exit
sources: Kahneman et al., When More Pain Is Preferred to Less (1993)
techniques.summary: Close a conversation while it is still fun, so the last impression is a good one.
techniques.why: The peak-end rule shows that people judge an experience largely by its best moment and its end, not its length. A thread that fizzles out leaves a flat memory; one that ends on a laugh or a warm line leaves them wanting more.
steps: Notice the high point: a laugh, a warm moment, a plan agreed.
Exit within a message or two of it.
Give a reason and a forward hook: "Off to cook. More later."
Don't restart the thread just because it's quiet.

examples.flat: (Keeps chatting until replies are "lol" and "ok")
examples.better: "Okay, I'm going before I say something that gets me in trouble at work. Tonight."
examples.note: Leaving on a playful note keeps the charge alive till evening.

examples.flat: Anyway, night.
examples.better: "Going to sleep now, smiling. Thanks to you."
examples.note: A warm final line becomes the memory of the whole conversation.

examples.flat: So yeah... what else is new?
examples.better: "That's the best thing I've read all week. Leaving on that. Talk tomorrow."
examples.note: Exiting at the high stops the thread sagging.

examples.flat: Any other business? No? Okay then, I guess that's it.
examples.better: "Great call. Three actions, all owned. Let's finish ten minutes early."
examples.note: Ending on a crisp win makes people remember the meeting fondly.

examples.flat: So, anything else we need to cover?
examples.better: "We're agreed on the main terms. Let's stop on that and send paperwork tomorrow."
examples.note: Closing at agreement avoids reopening settled points.

examples.flat: (Stays at the party until everyone is tired)
examples.better: "Best night in ages. I'm leaving while it's still perfect."
examples.note: Leaving at the peak makes the night feel legendary.

examples.flat: Okay well I guess I'll let you go.
examples.better: "I'm calling it here while you still think I'm funny. Thursday?"
examples.note: A self-aware exit with a next step leaves her wanting more.

mistakes: Exiting abruptly without warmth, which reads as offence.
Using exits as a power game to always have the last word.
Leaving in the middle of something they care about.
Never staying long enough to have a high point.

drills.prompt: Your partner just sent a great joke while you're both at work. Write an exit message.
models: "That's the one. I'm leaving on that. Tonight you owe me the full version."
"Okay, you win today. Back to work before I get caught grinning."

drills.prompt: End a client email thread on a high after a deal is agreed.
models: "Delighted we're aligned. Paperwork tomorrow, champagne later."
"Perfect. That's a great place to stop. I'll send the draft in the morning."

quiz.scenario: A text chat with your partner has just peaked with a big laugh. What is the best move?
options: Keep it going until you both run out of things to say.
Wrap up warmly with a hook for later.
Stop replying without saying anything.
Start a serious topic to balance it out.
quiz.why: The peak-end rule says the ending shapes the memory; leave on the high with a reason to come back.

quiz.scenario: Which closing line best follows the peak-end principle at work?
options: Okay, I guess we're done.
Sorry this ran over.
Any final thoughts? Anyone? Okay.
Great progress today. Two wins, one next step. Thanks, all.
quiz.why: It ends crisply on the achievement, so people remember the meeting as productive.

techniques.ethics: Leave on a high to share good feeling; disappearing to make someone chase you is a game, not a technique.

techniques.name: The Playful One-Liner & Callback
techniques.summary: Send short, playful lines that reference something you shared earlier, so the chat feels like a running private story.
techniques.why: A callback proves you were listening and remembered, which feels like attention. Comedians use callbacks because a returning joke gets a bigger laugh than a new one. In text, a quick, playful line lightens the mood and invites the other person to play back.
steps: Collect small, specific moments from your conversations.
Bring one back later in an unexpected context.
Keep the line short; the reference does the work.
Leave room for them to play back instead of explaining the joke.

examples.flat: How's your day?
examples.better: "Did the printer apologise yet, or are you still at war?"
examples.note: Referencing her morning complaint shows you remembered and makes her smile.

examples.flat: I'm looking forward to tonight.
examples.better: "Tonight's dress code: whatever you wore that made me miss my train."
examples.note: A playful callback to a shared memory adds a flirtatious charge.

examples.flat: What do you want for dinner?
examples.better: "Pasta, but not the cursed recipe from last Tuesday."
examples.note: An in-joke turns a logistics question into a moment.

examples.flat: Thanks for fixing the bug.
examples.better: "The gremlin has been banished. Again. You're a legend."
examples.note: A team callback adds warmth to routine thanks.

examples.flat: Let's discuss the timeline.
examples.better: "Ideally a timeline less dramatic than your airport story."
examples.note: A light callback to small talk builds rapport before business.

examples.flat: Are you coming on Saturday?
examples.better: "Coming Saturday? I promise no karaoke. Probably."
examples.note: A shared memory makes the invite feel personal and fun.

examples.flat: Hi, how are you?
examples.better: "Update: I tried the hot sauce you recommended. I may need a lawyer."
examples.note: Calling back her recommendation shows interest and invites a playful reply.

mistakes: Using inside jokes in a group chat where others are lost.
Explaining the joke after you send it.
Calling back something that was painful or embarrassing for them.
Relying only on wit and never saying anything sincere.

drills.prompt: Earlier your partner said she'd "fight anyone" for the last croissant. Write a callback text later that day.
models: "Bought two croissants. Nobody has to get hurt tonight."
"Croissant security has been arranged for tomorrow morning."

drills.prompt: Your colleague said in a meeting their laptop "has a personality." Write a callback message.
models: "How's the laptop's mood today? Need me to bring it a treat?"

drills.prompt: Reply with a playful one-liner when your partner texts: "I'm bored."
models: "Dangerous. Bored people end up with my full attention later."
"Want me to send you a riddle or a compliment? You only get one."

quiz.scenario: Why do callbacks work so well in texting?
options: They prove you remembered and create a running shared story.
They are always funny, even out of context.
They let you avoid real conversation.
They make the chat longer.
quiz.why: A callback signals attention and builds a private history between you.

quiz.scenario: Which is the best callback to a partner who mentioned a terrible work meeting this morning?
options: How was your day?
Meetings are boring for everyone.
You should have prepared better.
Did the meeting finally end, or are you still trapped there?
quiz.why: It references her specific moment with light humour and warmth.

techniques.ethics: Tease with, never at: a callback that pokes a real insecurity is negging in disguise.

techniques.name: Voice Notes vs Text
techniques.aka: Choosing the channel, when tone matters
sources: Kumar & Epley, It's Surprisingly Nice to Hear You (2021)
Kruger et al., Egocentrism Over E-mail (2005)
Schroeder & Epley, The Sound of Intellect (2015)
techniques.summary: Switch from text to voice note or call when warmth, nuance or emotion matter, and keep text for logistics and quick play.
techniques.why: Studies show people overestimate how well their tone carries in writing, so sarcasm and warmth are often misread. Experiments by Kumar and Epley found that people expect voice contact to be awkward, but it creates more connection than text without being as awkward as expected. A voice carries warmth, humour and intent that text can't.
steps: Ask: is this about logistics or feelings? Feelings go to voice.
Send a short voice note (under a minute) for warmth, apology or excitement.
Call for anything that could be misread or is emotional.
Keep text for confirmations, links and quick, light play.

examples.flat: Text: "Miss you."
examples.better: Voice note, quiet and smiling: "I just wanted you to hear me say it. I miss you. See you tonight."
examples.note: Hearing your voice turns a stock phrase into a felt moment.

examples.flat: Text: "Sorry about earlier."
examples.better: Call: "I was short with you this morning, and that wasn't fair. I'm sorry."
examples.note: Apologies land better in a voice, where sincerity is audible.

examples.flat: Text: "Good night."
examples.better: Ten-second voice note: "Good night, gorgeous. Sleep well."
examples.note: A sleepy voice note is more intimate than any emoji.

examples.flat: A long email arguing about a misunderstanding.
examples.better: "Can we jump on a quick call? I think we're closer than these emails make it sound."
examples.note: Moving off text defuses conflict that writing tends to escalate.

examples.flat: Email: "That's not acceptable."
examples.better: Call: "I want to understand what's driving this number. Talk me through it?"
examples.note: Voice lets you be firm and warm at once.

examples.flat: Text: "Happy birthday!!"
examples.better: Voice note singing badly: "Happy birthday, terrible singer included free."
examples.note: A personal voice note stands out among a hundred texts.

examples.flat: Text: "Hope you're ok."
examples.better: Call your parent: "No reason. Just wanted to hear your voice."
examples.note: A spontaneous call means more than a check-in text.

mistakes: Five-minute rambling voice notes nobody can skim.
Arguing over text when a call would settle it in two minutes.
Sending voice notes when the other person is at work and can't listen.
Using sarcasm in text and assuming the tone will carry.

drills.prompt: Write a 15-second voice note script for your partner on a stressful day.
models: "Hey. I know today's a lot. Just wanted you to know I'm proud of you, and dinner is handled. Come home and do nothing."

drills.prompt: A colleague has replied curtly to your email twice. Write the message that moves the conversation to voice.
models: "I think email is making this harder than it needs to be. Five minutes on a call?"
"Feels like we're talking past each other. Free for a quick call at three?"

quiz.scenario: You want to tell your partner how much last night meant to you. Which channel is best?
options: A long text paragraph.
An emoji.
A short voice note or saying it in person.
An email.
quiz.why: Emotional content carries best through voice, where warmth and sincerity can be heard.

quiz.scenario: What did Kumar and Epley's research find about voice versus text?
options: People expect voice to be awkward, but it creates more connection than they predict.
Text creates stronger bonds than calls.
Voice and text feel the same to recipients.
People always prefer calls.
quiz.why: Their experiments found people underestimate how connected a voice conversation makes them feel.

techniques.ethics: Choose voice for clarity and warmth; don't use calls to avoid leaving a record of commitments you should keep in writing.

techniques.name: Timing & Rhythm
techniques.aka: No games, no flooding, matching pace
techniques.summary: Reply at a natural, honest pace and roughly match the other person's rhythm, without playing waiting games or flooding them.
techniques.why: Gottman's work describes small "bids" for attention, and turning toward them builds trust; leaving them unanswered on purpose erodes it. At the same time, a wall of messages can overwhelm. Matching length and pace signals that you're in step, which feels like rapport.
steps: Reply when you're actually free; don't time replies to look busy.
Roughly match their message length and frequency.
If you can't reply properly, send a holding line: "Busy, will reply tonight."
Don't send a second message until they've answered the first, unless it's logistics.

examples.flat: (Ignores her text for hours to seem busy)
examples.better: "In meetings till four, thinking about you in between. Talk properly later."
examples.note: A quick holding line respects her bid without game-playing.

examples.flat: Five messages in a row: "Hey" "Hello?" "You there?" "??" "Ok then"
examples.better: One message: "Hey you. Call me when you're free?" Then wait.
examples.note: One calm bid shows security, not anxiety.

examples.flat: A 300-word reply to "Haha nice"
examples.better: "Right? Made my day."
examples.note: Matching her short energy keeps the chat light.

examples.flat: Replying to every Slack message instantly at midnight.
examples.better: "Got this. I'll reply properly first thing tomorrow."
examples.note: Healthy rhythm sets sustainable expectations.

examples.flat: Countering their offer within seconds.
examples.better: "Thanks for this. Let me review with the team and come back tomorrow morning."
examples.note: A deliberate pause signals seriousness and avoids rushed concessions.

examples.flat: (Leaves a friend's news on read for a week)
examples.better: "Just saw this! Congratulations. Proper reply when I'm off the train."
examples.note: A quick acknowledgement turns toward the bid even when busy.

examples.flat: Waiting exactly three days to text after a date.
examples.better: Next day: "Had a great time. Thinking about that ridiculous dessert."
examples.note: Honest timing reads as confidence, not desperation.

mistakes: Strategic delays to seem less interested.
Flooding someone with messages when they're quiet.
Reading too much into slow replies; people are busy.
Never replying properly because you only send holding lines.

drills.prompt: Your partner texted a photo of her new haircut while you're in a meeting. Write a holding reply.
models: "Stop it. Gorgeous. In a meeting, full reaction later."
"Very distracting. Proper compliments at seven."

drills.prompt: You've sent a message and she hasn't replied for two hours. Write what you do next.
models: Nothing. She's busy. Carry on with your day.
If it's logistics only: "No rush, just need to know about dinner by six."

quiz.scenario: What is the healthiest way to handle a text you can't fully answer right now?
options: Leave it until you have time, however long that takes.
Wait three hours so you don't seem keen.
Send a quick holding line and reply properly later.
Reply with a single emoji and forget it.
quiz.why: A holding line turns toward the bid honestly and sets an expectation.

quiz.scenario: Your date sends short, playful replies. How should you match her?
options: Write long paragraphs to show effort.
Keep your replies short and playful too.
Stop replying so she chases you.
Send several messages for each of hers.
quiz.why: Matching length and tone signals you're in step and keeps the exchange easy.

techniques.ethics: Honest pacing respects both people; manufactured silences or delays to create insecurity are manipulation.

techniques.name: The Assumptive, Specific Invitation
techniques.summary: Invite people with a specific day, time and plan, framed confidently, while making it easy to say no.
techniques.why: Research on implementation intentions shows that plans tied to a when and where are far more likely to happen. A specific invite also takes the planning load off the other person, so saying yes is easy. Confidence reads as attractive, and an easy out keeps it respectful.
steps: Name the day, time and place: "Thursday, eight, the Thai place."
Frame it as a plan, not a vague wish.
Add one hook that makes it appealing.
Give an easy out: "If not, Sunday works too."

examples.flat: We should go out sometime.
examples.better: "Saturday. Dinner at the place by the river, then a walk home the long way. I've booked eight."
examples.note: A full plan shows effort and makes the evening something to anticipate.

examples.flat: Want to do something this weekend?
examples.better: "Sunday morning: you, me, pancakes in bed. Very little clothing. The plan is non-negotiable."
examples.note: Playful, specific and assumptive, while clearly a tease she can laugh off.

examples.flat: Wanna hang out?
examples.better: "Drinks Thursday at seven? I'll grab the table by the window."
examples.note: Specific details make yes the easy answer.

examples.flat: Let's catch up soon.
examples.better: "Coffee Tuesday at ten? I'll come to your floor."
examples.note: A concrete plan turns small talk into an actual meeting.

examples.flat: Let's find a time to talk.
examples.better: "I'm holding Thursday at two to finalise terms. Does that work, or is Friday morning better?"
examples.note: Two specific options keep momentum while offering choice.

examples.flat: We should hike sometime.
examples.better: "Hike on Saturday, leaving at nine. I'll drive. Bring snacks."
examples.note: Clear logistics remove every excuse to delay.

examples.flat: We should get a drink sometime.
examples.better: "Let's get a drink. Wednesday at seven at Lumen? If that doesn't work, pick a night."
examples.note: Confident and specific with an easy out is ideal for an early date.

mistakes: Being so assumptive that no isn't a real option.
Vague invites ("sometime") that never become plans.
Asking open-ended questions like "When are you free?" that hand them the work.
Taking a decline personally rather than offering another time.

drills.prompt: Turn this into a specific invitation for a partner: "We should do a date night soon."
models: "Friday, seven-thirty. I've booked the tapas place. You just have to show up looking like that."
"Thursday night is ours. Dinner, then the jazz bar. Say yes."

drills.prompt: Turn this into a specific invitation for a colleague: "We should talk about the project."
models: "Can we take thirty minutes Wednesday at eleven to plan the next phase?"
"Lunch Friday? I'll bring the roadmap, you bring opinions."

quiz.scenario: Which invitation is most likely to turn into a real plan?
options: We should get dinner sometime.
Dinner Thursday at eight at Rosa's? If not, Sunday works.
When are you free?
Let me know if you ever want to hang out.
quiz.why: It is specific, appealing and gives an easy out, so yes is simple.

quiz.scenario: What keeps an assumptive invitation respectful?
options: Repeating it until they say yes.
Booking without telling them.
Saying you'll be upset if they decline.
Offering an easy alternative or way to say no.
quiz.why: Assumptive framing is about confidence, but the other person must always be free to decline.

techniques.ethics: Be confident in the ask and gracious with a no; pressuring, guilt or treating a decline as negotiable crosses the line.

modules.title: Shields: Spot Manipulation
modules.tagline: Recognise the tactic, stay calm, answer on your terms.
modules.intro: Knowing how influence works also means spotting when it's used against you. Each technique here names a manipulative tactic, shows lines you might hear, and trains a calm, strong response. In the examples, the first line is the tactic and the second is your counter.

techniques.name: False Urgency
sources: Worchel, Lee & Adewole, Effects of supply and demand on ratings of object value (1975)
FTC, Bringing Dark Patterns to Light (2022)
techniques.summary: Spot when someone invents a deadline or a shortage to stop you thinking, and buy back your time.
techniques.why: Scarcity and deadlines trigger fear of missing out, which narrows attention and speeds up decisions; studies show things simply seem more valuable when they seem scarce. Naming the pressure and slowing down restores your judgement. Genuine offers usually survive a 24 hour pause.
steps: Notice the squeeze words: now, only today, last one, don't tell anyone.
Ask yourself: what actually happens if I wait?
Say you decide on your own timeline.
If the offer vanishes, let it go.

examples.flat: This price is only good if you sign today.
examples.better: Then I'll miss it. I don't sign anything on the day I first see it.
examples.note: Calls the bluff calmly; real deals come back.

examples.flat: I need this approved in ten minutes or we lose the client.
examples.better: Send me what the client actually said and I'll look now. I won't approve it blind.
examples.note: Checks the urgency is real before acting.

examples.flat: I'm only in town this week, so we need to move fast.
examples.better: Then let's enjoy the week, at my pace.
examples.note: Keeps the fun and refuses to be rushed.

examples.flat: If you don't decide about moving in by Friday, I'm done.
examples.better: That's a big decision and I want to make it well. I'll have an answer in two weeks, and I'd love to talk it through before then.
examples.note: Respects the relationship but not the ultimatum's clock.

examples.flat: Only three spots left in the investment, are you in or out?
examples.better: Out, then. If it's good, it'll still be good next month.
examples.note: Treats manufactured scarcity as a red flag.

examples.flat: Gran, it's me, I need money sent right now, and please don't tell Mum.
examples.better: I'll call you back on your usual number.
examples.note: Urgency plus secrecy is a classic scam; verify through a channel you trust.

examples.flat: Your account will be closed in 1 hour. Click here to verify.
examples.better: (Don't click.) Open the bank's app yourself and check there.
examples.note: Phishing runs on false urgency; go around the link.

mistakes: Arguing about the deadline instead of simply declining.
Feeling rude for asking for time.
Assuming every deadline is fake; some are real.
Deciding fast just to avoid looking indecisive.

drills.prompt: Respond to: 'Another buyer is coming at three, so if you want the car I need a deposit now.'
models: Then sell it to them if they're ready. I'll decide after a mechanic has looked at it.
Understood. I don't pay deposits before an inspection.

drills.prompt: A date says: 'I'm leaving for months soon, so it's now or never with us.'
models: Then it might be never, and that's ok. I don't rush things that matter.
I like you. I'm still going at my speed.

quiz.scenario: A salesperson says: 'This deal expires at midnight.' Best response?
options: Buy now before it's gone
Sheepishly ask for an extension
I don't decide under deadlines. If it's gone, it's gone.
Accuse them of lying
quiz.why: Calm and unbothered: you keep your timeline without starting a fight.

quiz.scenario: Which combination is the strongest sign of a scam?
options: Urgency plus secrecy
A written quote
An offer to think it over
A follow-up email next week
quiz.why: Pressure to act now and keep it quiet is designed to stop you checking with anyone.

techniques.ethics: Real deadlines can be stated honestly; invented ones designed to stop you thinking are manipulation.

techniques.name: Guilt Tripping
sources: Baumeister, Stillwell & Heatherton, Guilt: an interpersonal approach (1994)
techniques.summary: Recognise when someone uses your guilt to steer you, and answer with care for them but no change to your decision.
techniques.why: Guilt is a strong social lever; research shows people use it, sometimes deliberately, to get others to do what they want. The way out is to separate their feelings, which you can acknowledge, from your choice, which stays yours. That breaks the lever without being cold.
steps: Notice the move: sacrifice, suffering, or 'after all I've done'.
Acknowledge their feeling in one sentence.
Restate your decision kindly.
Don't over-explain or defend.
Offer something you genuinely want to give, if anything.

examples.flat: After everything I've done for you, you can't come for one Sunday?
examples.better: I know you'd love me there, and I'm grateful for everything. I can't this Sunday. Can I come next week?
examples.note: Gratitude and the decision both stay intact.

examples.flat: Fine, go out with your friends. I'll just sit here alone.
examples.better: I can hear you'd like me home. I'm going for a couple of hours, and tomorrow night is ours.
examples.note: Warm and firm, with real connection on offer.

examples.flat: I guess I'll stay till midnight again, since nobody else cares.
examples.better: Sounds like you're overloaded. Let's look at what can move. I can't stay late tonight.
examples.note: Takes the real problem seriously without accepting the blame.

examples.flat: Wow. I thought you were a real friend.
examples.better: I am, and I'm still saying no to this one.
examples.note: Doesn't take the bait about who you are.

examples.flat: You'll put my family out of business with this price.
examples.better: I don't want that. This is our price. Let's see if a smaller order works for you.
examples.note: Empathy without caving.

examples.flat: I came all this way and you won't even let me stay over?
examples.better: I'm glad you came, and no, not tonight.
examples.note: Short, kind and final.

examples.flat: Guess I'm not important enough for a reply.
examples.better: You are. I was at work. I'll call you at seven.
examples.note: Answers the feeling and ignores the hook.

mistakes: Over-explaining, which invites more negotiation.
Getting angry, which proves their 'you don't care' story.
Caving, then resenting it.
Treating every hurt feeling as a guilt trip; sometimes people are simply hurt.

drills.prompt: Respond to: 'I suppose I'll just spend my birthday alone, then.'
models: I'd hate that. I can't do Saturday, but I'm taking you to lunch on Sunday.
I can tell you're disappointed. I'm still not free Saturday. How about Sunday?

drills.prompt: A colleague says: 'I covered for you last month, the least you can do is take my shift.'
models: You did, and I appreciate it. I can't do this shift. I can do next Tuesday's.
I owe you one and I'll repay it, just not this weekend.

quiz.scenario: Your mum says: 'I'll just eat Christmas dinner alone, don't worry about me.' Best response?
options: Fine.
Ok, I'll cancel my plans.
You're being so dramatic.
I don't want you alone. We're with Sarah's family this year, and we'll come to you on Boxing Day.
quiz.why: It shows care and offers something real, while keeping the original decision.

quiz.scenario: What is the key to resisting a guilt trip?
options: Give a long, detailed explanation
Acknowledge their feeling but keep your decision
Loudly point out that they're manipulating you
Agree, then quietly don't show up
quiz.why: Separating their feelings from your choice keeps both the relationship and the boundary.

techniques.ethics: Saying you're hurt is honest; using hurt as a lever to override someone's choice is manipulation.

techniques.name: Negging & Backhanded Compliments
sources: Sezer, Brooks & Norton, Backhanded compliments: how negative comparisons undermine flattery (2018)
techniques.summary: Recognise praise with a hidden dig, and respond without taking the hook or getting defensive.
techniques.why: Negging, a pick-up tactic popularised in the 2000s, mixes praise with a small dig so the target tries to win approval to fix it. Research on backhanded compliments found that people actually like the giver less, so you don't need to fight. A calm, amused non-reaction or a simple question exposes it.
steps: Spot the shape: praise plus a comparison, or 'for a...'.
Don't chase their approval or justify yourself.
Choose: accept only the compliment, ask a light question, or name it calmly.
Move on, or move away.

examples.flat: You're pretty, for someone who clearly isn't into fitness.
examples.better: Thanks. What a strange way to finish a sentence.
examples.note: Amused, not wounded, so the dig falls flat.

examples.flat: Your nails are cute. Are they real?
examples.better: Real enough. So what do you do when you're not reviewing manicures?
examples.note: Playful deflection without seeking approval.

examples.flat: Great presentation. I didn't expect that from you.
examples.better: What did you expect?
examples.note: A calm, curious question makes them explain the dig.

examples.flat: You're so articulate! (said with surprise)
examples.better: Thanks. I'd rather hear what you thought of the proposal.
examples.note: Redirects to the substance.

examples.flat: You look so much better than last time. You'd really let yourself go.
examples.better: I feel good, thanks. How's the garden?
examples.note: Takes the compliment, skips the dig, moves on.

examples.flat: I love that you don't care what people think of your clothes.
examples.better: I care what I think. And I love this jacket.
examples.note: Owns it with confidence.

examples.flat: You're actually smart, for once.
examples.better: That stung a little. I know you meant it as a joke, but can we drop the 'for once'?
examples.note: With someone close, name it kindly so it doesn't become a pattern.

examples.flat: Wow, you look good in this pic, way better than in person lol
examples.better: Ha. I'll take the first half.
examples.note: Light and unbothered, with no chasing.

mistakes: Laughing along, then stewing on it later.
Over-justifying ('I DO go to the gym').
Firing back an insult.
Ignoring a pattern from someone close to you.

drills.prompt: Respond to: 'You're braver than me, I could never wear that.'
models: Thanks, I love it.
It takes no bravery at all. Just good taste.

drills.prompt: On a date, they say: 'You're interesting. Not my usual type, though.'
models: Then this should be a fun experiment.
Good. Your usual type clearly wasn't working.

quiz.scenario: A colleague says: 'Good job, you finally got one right.' Best counter?
options: Thanks so much!
Well, you're not perfect either.
Thanks. What do you mean by 'finally'?
Say nothing and stew
quiz.why: A calm question accepts nothing and makes them own the dig.

quiz.scenario: Why do negs work on some people?
options: They're very funny
They make the target try to win approval to fix the small dig
They're honest feedback
They build trust
quiz.why: The tactic relies on unsettling confidence so the target chases; not chasing defuses it.

techniques.ethics: Teasing between people who like each other is play; a dig meant to lower someone's confidence so they'll chase you is manipulation.

techniques.name: Love Bombing
sources: Strutzenberg et al., Love-bombing: a narcissistic approach to relationship formation (2017)
techniques.summary: Notice when intense affection, gifts and future plans arrive faster than trust could, and set your own pace.
techniques.why: Flooding someone with early attention creates a feeling of debt and specialness that can make later control easier. Early research links love bombing with narcissistic traits and low self-esteem, though the evidence base is still small. The defence isn't suspicion of warmth; it's checking whether the pace respects your no.
steps: Notice the speed: 'soulmate' talk, big gifts, constant texts, big plans in week one.
Enjoy the warmth, but set your own pace.
State one small boundary and watch the reaction.
Judge them by how they handle your no, not by how big their yes is.

examples.flat: I've never felt this way. Let's go to Paris next month, I've already booked it.
examples.better: That's lovely, and it's too fast for me. Let's do dinner next week.
examples.note: Keeps the warmth, sets the pace, and tests their respect.

examples.flat: Good morning beautiful. Where are you? Why haven't you replied? I miss you so much.
examples.better: I like hearing from you. I'm busy in the day, so I'll reply in the evenings.
examples.note: A clear rhythm shows whether they can respect it.

examples.flat: You're my soulmate. I knew the moment I saw you.
examples.better: I like you too. I'd like to get to know you before I decide about souls.
examples.note: Light humour slows the story down.

examples.flat: You're the only one who really gets me. The others are so fake.
examples.better: I'm glad we're close. I like the others too.
examples.note: Gently refuses the isolation hook.

examples.flat: You're the best hire I've ever made, you're family. Now, about this weekend...
examples.better: Thank you. I can't work this weekend, but I'll be in early on Monday.
examples.note: Accepts the praise and separates it from the ask.

examples.flat: We love you guys, we'll be partners for decades, so just sign the exclusivity clause.
examples.better: We love the relationship too. Let's start with a one year term and grow from there.
examples.note: Warmth doesn't buy a long commitment.

examples.flat: I bought you a necklace. Can we just forget about last night?
examples.better: Thank you. I still need us to talk about last night.
examples.note: Gifts don't replace repair.

mistakes: Treating all generosity as a red flag.
Feeling you owe them because they gave so much.
Explaining your boundary over and over.
Ignoring anger when you slow things down; that reaction is the real signal.

drills.prompt: After two dates they say: 'I've told my parents all about you, they want to meet you this weekend!'
models: That's sweet. It's early for me to meet parents. Let's keep it just us for a while.
I'm flattered. Not yet. Let's get to know each other first.

drills.prompt: A new friend says: 'I bought us concert tickets, so you have to come, I've already paid!'
models: That's generous, and I can't make it. Could you sell them or take someone else?
Thank you, but please check with me before buying things for me.

quiz.scenario: What best separates love bombing from ordinary enthusiasm?
options: They text often
They react badly when you set a small boundary
They pay you compliments
They plan a nice date
quiz.why: Enthusiastic people adjust to your pace; love bombers push back when you slow down.

quiz.scenario: Two weeks in, they say: 'Let's move in together.' Best response?
options: Yes, why not?
Absolutely not, you're crazy.
Ignore it and change the subject
I love how much you like me. It's too soon for me. Let's keep dating and see.
quiz.why: Warm, clear and paced: you keep the good feeling and your judgement.

techniques.ethics: Enthusiasm is fine; flooding someone with affection to create debt or speed past their judgement is manipulation.

techniques.name: DARVO & Gaslighting
techniques.aka: Deny, Attack, Reverse Victim and Offender; reality denial
sources: Freyd, Violations of power, adaptive blindness, and betrayal trauma theory (1997)
Harsey, Zurbriggen & Freyd, Perpetrator responses to victim confrontation (2017)
Harsey & Freyd, DARVO: what is the influence on perceived perpetrator and victim credibility? (2020)
techniques.summary: Recognise when a confrontation gets flipped so you end up apologising, or your memory gets questioned, and hold on to the original point.
techniques.why: DARVO, a pattern named by psychologist Jennifer Freyd, denies the issue, attacks the person raising it, then casts the offender as the victim. Studies link hearing it with more self-blame, and found that people who know about DARVO are less swayed by it. Gaslighting works by making you doubt your own perception, so notes and facts restore your footing.
steps: Write down what happened, soon after it happens.
Put your point in one sentence and keep returning to it.
Acknowledge their feelings without dropping your point.
State your memory once; don't debate it.
If it's a pattern, get outside support from someone you trust.

examples.flat: That never happened. You're always imagining things. Honestly, I'm the one who should be upset.
examples.better: I remember it clearly, and I'm not going to argue about my memory. I'm upset about what you said on Friday.
examples.note: States reality once and returns to the issue.

examples.flat: I never agreed to that deadline. Why are you attacking me in front of everyone?
examples.better: I'm not attacking you. Here's the email from the 3rd. Let's sort out the deadline.
examples.note: Facts and calm undercut the reversal.

examples.flat: Wow, after everything I've been through, you bring THIS up?
examples.better: I know you've had a hard time, and I care. I still need to talk about the money.
examples.note: Holds compassion and the point together.

examples.flat: You're too sensitive, it was a joke. Now you've ruined dinner.
examples.better: It may have been a joke to you. It hurt me. Saying so isn't ruining dinner.
examples.note: Rejects the reversal without escalating.

examples.flat: You're crazy. I never said I was single.
examples.better: You did, last Tuesday, and I have the messages. I'm done here.
examples.note: Short, factual, and you leave.

examples.flat: We never promised delivery by June, and frankly your accusation is insulting.
examples.better: Clause 4.2 says June. I'm not accusing you, I'm asking what you'll do about it.
examples.note: Points to the record and the request.

examples.flat: Stop twisting my words. You always make me the bad guy.
examples.better: I'm not trying to make you the bad guy. The comment upset me. Can we talk in person?
examples.note: Lowers the heat while keeping the point.

mistakes: Arguing every detail, so you lose the thread.
Apologising for raising the issue at all.
Doubting yourself without checking your notes.
Handling a repeated pattern alone instead of talking to someone you trust.

drills.prompt: Respond to: 'I can't believe you'd accuse me of that after all I do for you. You're the one with the problem.'
models: I'm not saying you're a bad person. What happened on Saturday hurt, and I want to talk about it.
I hear that you're hurt. My point still stands: the comment at the party wasn't ok.

drills.prompt: A colleague says: 'I never said you could take the lead. You're making things up again.'
models: We talked about it on the 12th and I sent a recap afterwards. Let's look at it together.
I have the recap email. If you've changed your mind, that's fine, let's talk about that instead.

quiz.scenario: What does DARVO stand for?
options: Deny, Attack, Reverse Victim and Offender
Defend, Agree, Resolve, Verify, Overcome
Doubt, Argue, Repeat, Validate, Object
Distract, Accuse, Retreat, Vent, Obey
quiz.why: Knowing the pattern by name makes it easier to spot, and research suggests it reduces its pull.

quiz.scenario: You raise a concern and they say: 'You're crazy, that never happened, and I'm hurt you'd even say it.' Best move?
options: Apologise for upsetting them
Spend an hour proving your memory
State your memory once, acknowledge their feelings, and return to your concern
Keep shouting until they admit it
quiz.why: You stay anchored to the issue without getting pulled into a fight about reality.

techniques.ethics: Disagreeing about what happened is normal; denying someone's reality and flipping the blame to escape accountability is manipulation.

techniques.name: Pressure Past a No
techniques.aka: Foot-in-the-door abuse, the low-ball, wearing you down
sources: Freedman & Fraser, Compliance without pressure: the foot-in-the-door technique (1966)
Cialdini et al., Low-ball procedure for producing compliance (1978)
techniques.summary: Spot when small yeses are being stacked into a big one, or a no is treated as an opening bid, and make your no stick.
techniques.why: Agreeing to a small request makes us more likely to agree to a bigger one, because we like to act consistently with what we've already done. Pressure tactics also use fatigue: they keep asking until refusing feels harder than giving in. Seeing the pattern lets you judge each ask on its own.
steps: Judge each request fresh: would I say yes if this were the first ask?
Say no once, briefly, without a reason they can argue with.
Repeat the same words calmly if they push.
End the conversation or leave if they keep going.

examples.flat: Come on, one more drink. Ok, just come up for a coffee. Just ten minutes.
examples.better: I've had a lovely time and I'm heading home. Goodnight.
examples.note: Clear and warm, with no gap to negotiate.

examples.flat: Since you've chosen the base model, you'll want the warranty, and the service plan, and...
examples.better: I agreed to the base model. That's what I'm buying.
examples.note: Separates the first yes from the add-ons.

examples.flat: You made the slides, so you might as well present them. And take the questions. And the follow-up.
examples.better: Happy with the slides. Presenting is a separate job, and I can't take it this week.
examples.note: Judges each ask on its own.

examples.flat: You said maybe! Maybe means yes, come on!
examples.better: Maybe meant I'd think about it. I've thought about it. No.
examples.note: Turns a maybe into a clean no.

examples.flat: Just sign here, it's only a formality, then we'll talk about the house.
examples.better: I don't sign anything I haven't read. Send it over and I'll get back to you.
examples.note: Refuses the small step toward a big commitment.

examples.flat: Why not? Give me one good reason.
examples.better: I don't need a good reason, I just don't want to. Let's pick something else.
examples.note: A no doesn't have to win a debate.

examples.flat: Pleeease. You owe me. Just this once.
examples.better: I've answered. Still no. Talk tomorrow.
examples.note: Repeats, closes, moves on.

mistakes: Giving reasons that invite counter-arguments.
Softening the no into a maybe.
Feeling you must stay consistent with an earlier yes.
Staying in the conversation long after the no.

drills.prompt: Respond to: 'You lent me fifty last week, so two hundred this week shouldn't be a big deal.'
models: Last week was last week. I can't lend two hundred.
No, I'm not able to. I hope you get it sorted.

drills.prompt: At a party, someone keeps topping up your glass after you've said you're done.
models: I'm done for tonight, thanks. (hand the glass back)
Still done. I'm going to grab some water.

quiz.scenario: Why does a small yes make a bigger yes more likely?
options: Small requests are always fair
People like to act consistently with what they've already agreed to
Big requests are more exciting
It's random
quiz.why: The consistency pull is what foot-in-the-door tactics exploit; judging each ask fresh breaks it.

quiz.scenario: Someone says: 'Why not? Give me one reason.' Best response?
options: List all your reasons
Agree to avoid conflict
Make up an excuse
I don't need a reason. No, thanks.
quiz.why: Reasons give them something to argue with; a calm no without one closes the door.

techniques.ethics: Asking again later is normal; treating a no as an obstacle to wear down is coercion.
